en: Oṃ. Salutations to the venerable gurus;
salutations to the illustrious Sundaragaṇapati.

The *Bṛhattālavidhi* (including the *Māsapūjā*, *Śāntihoma*, etc.
1) May there be auspiciousness!

The celebrated bull, with its renowned broad-hoofed legs, shining in the midst of its hooves, joined by the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), the one who holds the mountain of the world upon his horns, the flower of the quarters, the moon-flower, the moon, the *kutra*—[I praise] the Bull.

Having caused the bull, the vehicle and emblem of Śiva, to coil and uncoil; having caused Maḍi to whirl and Maḍi to whirl; being manifest as the bearer of Śiva, manifest, manifest; having laughed at the seizing of the cow by the planet [Rāhu], he recited the birth [of the child]... (2)

One should proclaim the portion-bliss, the supreme distinction, the five great sounds, the dance, the handful of flowers, and the excellent *vara-āṭi* of passion. [She who has] Brahmā, Vaiśravaṇa, and the golden rampart; whose face is like the moon with two eyes and a thousand rays; who holds a water-pot in her left hand and a rosary in her right hand as a boon-giver; who is mounted upon a swan below, crowned with matted locks, and always attended by the lords of sages—[O you] who have arisen from the festival and so forth, come quickly! [The practice of] Brahmā, restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and meditation (*dhyāna*)...

Endowed with the eight limbs accompanied by *naya* and *yoga-samādhi*, renowned for the attainment of the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṇimā*) and so forth, [he is] the one who has... the nectar of all the *Āgamas*... the abode of the fourfold truth and the unsurpassed truth in the world, [residing] on the banks of the Sarasvatī... fanned by the beautiful whisks moving like sprouts in the form of his beloved... having cast off the golden mountain-like body, [he is] the eternal, awakened, pure knowledge-essence, seated upon the lotus-throne... the sixty-four *Āgamas*.

He whose form consists of the totality of mantras, headed by the seventy million great mantras; who is joined by the assembly of sages such as Kauśika; who is accompanied by the host of deities of the site (vāstu) beginning with Īśāna; together with the entire multitude of Brahmās dwelling in the netherworlds (pātāla);
the beloved of the lotus, the supreme cause of causes, and so forth—the four-faced one.

Sundara-priya-sundara-priya-geya-nṛtta (3). Hiraṇyagarbha-pitāmaha; the sound of kettledrums, maddala drums, muraja drums, jhallari cymbals, conchs, and kāhalaka trumpets; uninterrupted by song and dance; known as the *brahmatāla*. That which is known as the *brahmatāla*—the *tāla* of the *brahmatāla*... the *gāva-kula* dance with feet together.
— *Paṇ* — the fifth musical note — the *śacchapuṭa* instrument.

[I bow] to him whose mind is satisfied by the pride of ascending the neck of Airāvata, who is as white as the moon, the Himalayas, the *kunda* flower, sandalwood, and nectar; who is worshipped by throngs of gods;
and whose broad, beautiful, and radiant breasts are firmly embraced by Gautama’s beloved wife.

I bow to the one who is playful and fond of sport, the three-footed Lord of the gods, marked with the thunderbolt; whose own body possesses the beauty of a thousand tender sprouts reddened by the mass of rays from the jeweled crowns of all the gods and asuras;
who has a thousand eyes in the form of a lotus made of the essence of beauty; whose limbs are enchanting, adorned with garlands of *pārijāta* flowers brought by the deities of the Nandana grove;

who dwells in the city of Amarāvatī, where the proud Valabhī pavilions on the banks are carried about by thousands of Brahmās and Viṣṇūs; whose chest is beautiful with the luster of the moon, jasmine, and sandalwood; and who is fragrant with the scent of swaying, fierce... [the wind].

He whose staff-like arms were adorned with the sharp support of the bow of the winged mountains, made proud by his palms as hard as they were when shattering the coastal cliffs of Airāvata—terrible with the application of ichor from his trunk;

he who, with the hollows of his hands, brought together and blended the sweet sounds of the *vallakī* lute along with all the natural melodies of the *mṛdaṅga*, *tāla*, and *śāpa*; he who, at the command of the Supreme Lord, protected the eastern quarter;

he who, together with the entire host of Indras and lords of the Gaṇas—including the twelve Ādityas, the nine planets, the lunar mansions, the zodiac signs, Urvaśī and others, and all the inhabitants of the divine atmosphere and the netherworld such as the lord of the Pātāla—[ruled] over the earth and the other seven worlds.

He who, with hands reaching out to touch the sprouts of the tree of reality, which has been made to blossom by the Lord of the Gods situated in the eastern quarter, [resides] beyond the city of the Lord...
In front of the sound of Śiva, who is like Indra, the Lord of the Gods,
[there was] passion, the Bhairava rhythm, the Sama rhythm, the serpent dance, the drum, and the music of Kāmeśa;
[by him] all this was pervaded for the sake of the seven-flamed one.
To him whose body has become the manifest form of the Lord, shining like a ram...

(I.8a) ...this world, consisting of moving and non-moving beings such as carnivorous creatures and others, does not exist apart from that Supreme One; [he who is] the one through whom the offerings of *havya* and *kavya*—which serve to satisfy the gods and ancestors—are presented, adorned by the multitude of lotus-like hands of Śaṅkara, and [who is] the source of the egg-born [beings]... the dispeller of the heat of the three worlds.

Agni is present here—he whose nature is to be meditated upon in three ways; who dwells in the city of Tejovatī; who, out of compassion for the cause of the actions of all people, is beloved by the goddess Svāhā; whose vehicle is eternally mounted upon a ram; who possesses a great power consisting of light that blazes like the fire of destruction at the end of an eon for the entire world; whose hand is praised as being well-armed with a great spear; who delights in the sweet sounds of the *tāla* and *varāṭī* drums struck by his steady hands; who is fond of the *kollī* melody; who is the lord of the southeastern quarter; and who is surrounded by a retinue including the sages Sanaka and others, their wives, and their sons. Saṃmi... (5)
The eye, reddened and weary with blood, seized by the crocodile-grasp of darkness;
the womb, filled with the clamor of the assembly of demons;
the hip, swollen and increased by the burning inflicted by the thunderbolt of Yama.

Haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ! (6) It has been stepped upon, it has been stepped upon, on the rugged slopes of the mountain-like face of the Preceptor of the Gods; indeed, on those very rugged slopes of the mountain-like face of the Preceptor of the Gods.

To the accompaniment of the *rāga* Varāṭī, the *tāla* Mattāvaraṇa, and the dance performed in the circular arena (*maṇḍala*), with the musical instruments *paṇava* and *kolli* struck together— Yama, mounted upon a buffalo, bearing a banner, a noose, and a staff, wrathful, terrifying to the world, with fierce eyes, and armed with the staff known as Kāla, accompanied by hosts of *bhūtas* and *pretas*, became the body of the Lord of Gods. May he [protect you].
Hara is to be served; let there be festivities and the like, and let everyone come together quickly.
The son of the moon and the sun who have settled upon every universe; he whose compassion extends to Mukunda, Indra, and the other gods; he who dwells in the city of Yama, the restrainer;

he who views with equanimity the entire web of moving and unmoving beings; he whose mount is a buffalo terrifying with its horns, which cause mountains and thunderbolts to tremble at his very breath; the crusher of the lineage of the demon Bhuvaṅkanda.

The Lord of the Southern Quarter, who holds a staff and is fond of the sounds of *bhṛṅgin*, *tāla*, *aṭṭahāsa*, *daṇḍapāṇi*, *kujjari*, *kauśika*, and others; who is surrounded by the entire host of primary attendants beginning with Vighneśvara and accompanied by the powers (*śakti*) of Brahmā and the other gods; together with the *yama-gaṇas*—resembling *sāridhārin*, *sāsārin*, *kahakaha*, and *kāka*; possessing a sharp sword as formidable as the night-stalker *Kumbhaniśācara* and the slow-moving mountain-dweller; dancing with feet like staffs and hands like *bhṛṅgin* and *tāla*; and [playing] the *paṇ-kauśika*.

— with cymbals sounding *malita* and *maṭṭaya* — he whose eyes are red like gold, followed by that younger brother [... the wind-god, bearing a sharp spear and a shield... mounted upon a corpse-drawn vehicle equipped for combat — accompanied by fanged, powerful Rākṣasas, O devotee, may that great protector [grant you] well-being! [He who wards off] death and old age corrupted by impure karma... (3)

Niṛti, the lord of the southern and western quarters, who delights in the sounds of dancing and terrifying speech that strikes fear into the serpents; whose palm is joined with a sword resembling the smoke from the breath of the serpent-king; whose mount is a swift Vetāla with thighs capable of leaping across the entire universe; who dwells in the city of Kṛṣṇāvatī; who is dear to the swarm of night-stalkers who set in motion unrighteousness and break the assembly of righteous people; who is the beloved of the bees that are the multitudes of disciplined beings led by the Lord of the Goad (Śiva), who is skilled in mounting the excellent training of thousands of those who have cast away the fear of illusion; and who is the object of prostration through the devotion of the devotees of Śiva.

I bow to him who is surrounded by hosts of great rākṣasas such as Nāmuci, Daityendra, Mukunda, Sarakunda, Surāri, Svarṇalocana, Mahājṛmbha, Śaṅkhukarṇa, Vairocana, Hayagrīva, Hiraṇyākṣa, and Hālāhala; who holds in his hand a sword that causes terror to the universe;

who bears a playful flash of light from eyes agitated by the destruction of the demon Kakṣamaṇi’s armpit; who possesses a trembling sword-blade made restless by the pride of the demon Sarabha; and whose lotus-face is praised for its manifest dancing with a slight frown.

Dark as the black bee, possessing a dark and languid splendor, with shimmering hair and a sapphire-blue hue; [he who is] that very one, ever-shimmering, possessing a dark and languid splendor, with shimmering hair and a sapphire-blue hue.
(3) With passion, the Bhairava rhythm, the Malla rhythm—dance accompanied by the terrifying sound of serpents, the Paṇ-naṭṭha dialect, and the Lambuka musical instrument.

Mounted upon the Makara, holding a noose, resembling a white water-lily, the moon, or a conch shell; adorned with armlets, gems, and pearls, surrounded by joyful gods amidst the roar of kettledrums and beautiful dancing. (5)

And Varuṇa, the lord of the gods, accompanied by Geya, who dwells in the city of Sarasvatī— the essence of all holy waters, the guardian of the jewel-treasury that is the nectar-like essence reviving the entire host of deities, the moon-stone for the rays of the Supreme Person which are the memory [of Him],

the one whose vehicle is the makara at the bottom of the entire ocean, the hand of the one who holds the noose resting upon the serpent, the lord of the regions of Nāga, Tāla, Siṃhala, and Kuñjara, [residing] at the Gaṅgā-tīrtha.

Accompanied by the goddess Virāj, surrounded by the host of Varuṇa together with the fourteen worlds, Varuṇa is present here. [... [He whose] waist-region is like a blooming bandhūka flower, whose beautiful body is adorned with a continuous, lovely neck, whose lotus-feet are marked by the restless *vindyā* [sign], whose neck is decorated with jewel-encrusted ornaments, who possesses the pride of the gods, demigods, and even the god of love himself, [he is held] in the palm of his hand... (3)
The playful sport in the ocean; that very [sport]—the playful sport in the ocean held in the palm of the hand; the melody (*rāga*) Kurjari; the rhythm (*tāla*) Nāgatāla; the dance Kuñcita;

the musical instrument (*paṇava*); the venerable Kāmara; the instrumental music Siṃhanāda; mounted upon a deer-vehicle, bearing a banner, adorned with the primordial ones (*ādibhiḥ*), and accompanied by the smoke-colored hosts of *dhūmarudgaṇas*.
The man is endowed with the peace of the Goddess; and Vāyu, who is the life-breath of the three worlds—Heaven, the Atmosphere, and the Earth—is likewise joined with her.
He supports the multitude of living beings through the fivefold vital breaths beginning with *prāṇa*.

He bears the weight of the seven worlds, which are bound together by the seven spinal columns (*skandha*). He possesses the splendor and majesty renowned in the realm of the Thousand-Eyed One (Indra). Adorned with a crown of matted locks, he is endowed with supreme fortune and the fragrance of the Gandharvas, and he dwells in the city of Gandhavatī.

The wind-god Vāyu, beloved by Keśin, who causes fear to the armies of Surasena, whose banners and weapons are gathered together, whose palms are joined in salutation, who delights in the regions of the forest-dwellers, and who is accompanied by Añjanā; the wind-god surrounded by the hosts of Maruts such as Kāli, Viśāca, and Camari— [he who is] entirely [pure],
seated upon a noble, intoxicated elephant, with a body as lofty as a lotus.

He is one whose mass of blossoms is shaken by the breeze from the saptala trees in full bloom; he wears earrings adorned with swarms of bees as his ornaments; he possesses a pair of hands holding a ḍamaru drum, and with that drum, he causes the surface of the earth to tremble during his dance; his feet are tawny like auspicious lotuses, most beautiful and charming with their tinkling bells; and he is intent on dancing to the sweet, resonant sounds produced by the clusters of shimmering jewels.
With his waist-cloth hanging down like a bee, he possesses a multitude of qualities;

on the surface of the earth, he [performs] the pair of Vedic words, the pair of those various Vedic words on the surface of the earth—the *rāga*, the *deśāgiri* and *balitāla* rhythms, the dance graceful as a serpent, the musical instrument *paṇaḥtakkeśi*, and the *japuṭa* chant. Mounted upon the excellent vehicle of the human being, he is adorned with jewels and other ornaments.

His body possessing the luster of cow’s milk, adorned with jewel-garments bestowed by the Lord of Wealth, accompanied by Gandharvas, Apsaras, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas, [he whose feet are worshipped by all the gods] such as Hari and Viriñca, whose power is difficult to behold and immeasurable, whose feet are served by all the deities presiding over the treasures beginning with Śaṅkha and Padma, whose majesty is sung by the hosts of Puṇyajanas in the gardens of Caitraratha and the ten pleasure-grounds, who dwells in the city of Alakā variegated by heaps of every kind of jewel, and whose heart is moved by the Goddess who dances with joy arising from the entire world— [he is the one].

As long as the beloved Lord Mevagaṃbhīra, mounted upon an elephant, holding a mace in his hand, having transcended all worldly calamities, fond of the *tāla* and *pañcama* scales, the *kuñcita-nṛtta*, the *mālava-giri-takka-śiśira* melody, and Kubera, the lord of the northern quarter—[who is] accompanied by the entire host of Kubera’s followers, such as the *kinnaras*, *kiṃpuruṣas*, and various *vidyādharas*—[and who is] like a divine [presence];

[he who is] auspicious with a radiance white as a shimmering water-lily, possessing all majesty, eternally seated upon a lotus whose petals are spread out, with eyes directed toward the entire creation; [May he grant] prosperity.

Accomplished and renowned, characterized by the excellence of the goals of human life, eternal, well-accumulated, and pure; protecting, desiring to speak, constant, marvelous, abundant, with excellent and beautiful umbrellas;
that which is variegated, praised, beautiful, and lovely; [with] the *rāga* Gauḍika, the *tāla* Gauḍikkaula, the dance *ākuñcita*, and the *paṇ*-instrumental music *kauśika*.

The fifth: He who resembles pure crystal, who bears the moon, who is served by Brahmā and the others, who is endowed with the eight forms such as the sky and so forth, and whose essence is the Īśāna mantra—may he be worshipped, he who is adorned with matted hair and a skull upon his right shoulder, and who is accompanied by the trident, fire, and serpents.

He whose pair of lotus-feet are to be worshipped by the entire host of gods and asuras; whose crest-jewel at the tip of his matted locks—flowering with the rays of the crescent moon—is encircled by the overflowing waters of the ocean; who is marked by a third eye that mocks the splendor of the rising sun; who is adorned with beautiful emerald ear-ornaments; whose natural appearance and dress possess the white hue of Śaradā’s hand; who resides in the city of Yaśovatī; whose banner is graced by the bull; and whose hands hold the stone trident that took the life of the enemy of the gods (Śiva).

Ishana, the lord of the north-eastern quarter, who delights in the sounds of the hand-drum (*ḍakkā*), the cymbals (*tāla*), and the water-jar (*kuṃbha*), and who performs the upward dance; he who is accompanied by the weapons of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, as well as the Pāśupata, Aghora, and Praty-aṅgirā weapons; surrounded by the hundred Rudras beginning with Kapālin; and who possesses the thirty-six [principles] contained within the twenty-eight great Tantras—characterized by the nature of the Lord (*pati*), the individual soul (*paśu*), and the fetter (*pāśa*), and consisting of conduct (*caryā*), ritual action (*kriyā*), yoga (*yoga*), and knowledge (*jñāna*)—[is present here]. O Kauśika, he who is endowed with a multitude of sages such as Ādi-ṛṣi, joined with all the lords... [he] is Hara, who is worshipped by the lotus-born Brahmā; whose neck resembles a conch shell (*kaṃbu*); whose hands, feet, and throat are adorned with tiny bells (*kiṃkiṇī*);
the Lord of the Lotus, who holds the auspicious leftward-turning lotus.
I worship him who is praised by the auspicious ones, who is victorious, and who removes [all suffering] again and again.
One should cause the five great sounds to resound: *rāga*, *kuṇḍīra*, *tāla*, *ḍhakkāri*, and *nṛttamūrdhapāda*; the hand-instrument *paṇ*, the *śālāpāṇi* instrument, and the *kumbhavādya*.
Thus ends the *Brahmatālavidhi*, which bears the name of the Supreme Lord.
May there be auspiciousness for the monthly festival.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the monthly worship:
the moment of the solar transit is subtle and difficult to perceive even for those with the eyes of a hawk.
Furthermore, through that conjunction, thirty pure nāḍīs follow thereafter; O twice-born ones,
it has been declared that the thirty nāḍīs on the right are for the future,
while those on the left are for the past.
The transits, the equinoxes, and especially the two solstices—when the sun is in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo; (3)

This is named Viṣṇupada; its fruit is greater than that of the Viṣuva. O twice-born ones, when the sun’s course is in Virgo, Gemini, Pisces, or Sagittarius, it is declared to be the Ṣaḍaśītimukha, which is most exceedingly meritorious.
Sixteen *nāḍīs* [precede] the transition from the former [sign] and sixteen follow it.
When Libra and Aries are present, there are ten *nāḍīs* on both sides.
Likewise, when Viṣṇu is present, there will be ten in the solstice (*ayana*).
Likewise, at the commencement of the six-aśīti periods, when the sun has passed [into a new sign], during the northern course of the sun,
at the sighting of Rāhu (an eclipse), at the transit of the sun, and on occasions of marriage, death, or prosperity.
In the case of optional vows (*kāmyavrata*) observed at night, one should perform acts such as bathing and giving gifts;

likewise, one should celebrate a festival for the deity and perform the worship of Śiva right there. Whatever [deities] are present... even at the time of the sun's passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), it is to be done as before.
Having consecrated the deity with the preliminary rites of bathing and so forth,

and having adorned the primary *liṅga* and other icons with all ornaments, one should lead [the image], together with the *bhakta-beras* such as Soma and Skanda, along with a village, a town, or a temple, in circumambulation.
Having first performed the lustration (*nirājana*) and other rites at the place of Brahmā or on the tip of the bull, one should install [the deity] in its own place.
When this is done in the kingdom, no monthly defect occurs.
Therefore, one should properly perform the festival with every effort.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the monthly festival.
The Fortnightly Festival. Now, the procedure for the fortnightly festival:
On the eighth part of the fourteenth day, the moon becomes waned.
Or else, on the eighth part of the new moon, the earth shall again become a stake.
The day on which the moon is visible is considered Asinīvālī; the day on which it has disappeared is considered Kuhū. That new moon day (Amāvāsyā) which occurs at midday continues thereafter.
That should be known as Bhūtavidyā; it occurs on the fifteenth lunar day.
Even if a single ghaṭikā of the new moon coincides with the first day of the lunar fortnight, then [it is so].
The science of spirits (bhūtavidyā) should also be performed during rites for the gods or the ancestors,
provided that the first lunar day (pratipad) or the new moon (amāvāsyā) extends into the forenoon.
That Bhūtavidyā should always be performed during rites for the gods in the signs of Libra, Capricorn, Pisces, Virgo, Aries, and Gemini; likewise,
Bhūtavidyā should also be diligently honored on the new moon day.
On this day, the fourteenth lunar tithi is complete, beginning with Nandā and leading to the Akṣaya day.

One should perform the festival of the deity on the fourteenth day, and the pilgrimage at the sacred ford on the new moon day; likewise on a Monday coinciding with the new moon, or on a Sunday coinciding with the seventh lunar day.
On a Tuesday falling on the fourth lunar day, the fruit is equal to that of the equinox (viṣuvat). On a Monday coinciding with the new moon, it shall be equal to Caturdaśī-Śivarātri.
One should keep a vigil at night and perform a festival for the deity.
If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) falls on a Monday in conjunction with the constellation Ārdrā,
one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices, austerities, and gifts through that vow.
Furthermore, on that new moon day, [the rites for] the installation, de-installation, and the portable image (bera) of the Mūla-liṅga and others [should be performed].

Having performed the great consecration preceded by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), having adorned [the deity] with all ornaments, and having offered the great oblation (*mahāhavis*), one should lead the Lord in circumambulation through villages, market towns, and the like, accompanied by the procession of offerings (*balibhramaṇa*), together with a parasol, chowries, and so forth, along with many various lamps and various musical instruments. (7)
Having brought [the deity] to the station of Brahmā and having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājanā) and other rites as before, one should establish [the deity] in its own place.
Thus, whatever mortal performs this shall attain a meritorious state;
one desiring a son obtains sons, and one desiring a daughter obtains an auspicious daughter.

One who seeks wealth shall obtain abundant riches; one who seeks liberation shall attain liberation. Just as the rain-cloud does not fail to rain at the proper time, so too a man shall be freed from calamities. By fasting on the new moon day alone, one shall obtain all desires.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the New Moon festival.

Now follows the ritual for the full moon day (*paurṇimā-vidhi*). (3) The full moon day is considered to be of two kinds: *rākā* and *anumatī*. That which occurs earlier is *anumatī*, and the one following it is *rākā*.
The end of the fortnight, known as the fifteenth day, is remembered as the full moon (paurṇamāsī).
On the sixteenth day, [the rite] is desired; the midday occurs on the fifteenth day.

The fourteenth day is the least auspicious; it is sinful on the seventeenth day. All days from the first lunar day (pratipad) through the fourteenth (bhūta) are [auspicious], from sunrise until sunrise.
Known as Saṃpūrṇā, it is purifying and performed by the gods;
it belongs to Yama, Agni, Yama, the Bhūtas, the six sages, Vasu, and Indra.
(6) The twelfth lunar day is joined with Rudra, and the full moon day with the fourteenth.
The science of spirits (bhūtavidyā) also [teaches] that a sacrifice on the day of the new moon yields great fruit.
There too, as before, having performed the ritual actions up to the offering of food (*naivedya*), preceded by the worship of Vighneśa;
and having led Vighneśa and all the other deities, adorned with every ornament, in a circumambulation starting from the east;
one should re-establish them in their own places as previously described.
By the command of Śiva, all defects arising from omissions or interruptions in the ritual procedure shall perish.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the Full Moon Festival.
Now, the ritual procedure for the festival of the lunar mansions (*ṛkṣotsava*). (2) Now, worship performed under all the lunar mansions is dear to Śiva;
O twice-born ones, I shall explain its fruit in brief as I have heard it from Hara.
The lunar day (*vāra*) is said to possess one-fold merit, while the lunar date (*tithi*) possesses ten-fold merit;
the conjunction (*yoga*) is ten times more meritorious than that, and the lunar phase (*karaṇa*) is said to be even more so than that.
Therefore, the *lagna* is ten times more significant than that, and the *nakṣatra* yields even greater fruit.
(4) Where, by means of the two [planetary] statements, one leads the sun from its setting to its rising with the moon.
In that very place one should fast during the asterism, except for Śravaṇā,
from the time after sunset until three nāḍīs before sunrise.
One should fast at that very [lunar mansion], and perform the bath and worship there;
or else, whichever lunar mansion is reached during the day before the full moon,
one should perform the fast, worship, bath, and gift-giving there.
If there is a double aspect within a single month, the former should be accepted and not the latter.
The Uttarāyaṇa, the Yoga-yukta, and likewise the Vāyana;
or even the Saṃkrānti and the Grahaṇa occurring on a day joined with the feet of Hari.

O best of sages, one should perform the pilgrimage at the time of the evening when the constellation is preeminent, during a festival dedicated to the gods and for the sake of the supreme object of attainment, provided it is a pervasive [auspicious] moment.
Having worshipped Śiva under the asterism Kṛttikā, one becomes endowed with wealth, grain, and other riches;
having enjoyed supreme happiness in this world, one attains union [with the Divine] at the end.
(2) For the sake of destroying untimely death, one should worship Śaṅkara under the asterism Rohiṇī.
Having worshipped Īśvara in the north, those of great strength and prowess [proceeded].
That best of practitioners shall become vigorous and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge;
by worshipping Hara under the constellation Ārdrā, he obtains all prosperity.
One born under Punarvasu is worthy of worship and destroys his enemies along with his kinsmen;
one born under Puṣya gains nourishment of the body and excellent sons.
There, the worshiper of the Lord of Gods obtains many sons;
having worshipped Śiva under the Maghā asterisms, one becomes preeminent among one's own kin.
When joined with the five [asterisms] beginning with Pārśva, there is good fortune in Pūrvaphalgunī;
in Uttaraphalgunī, there is wealth, grain, divine jewels, and much that is given as a gift.
By worshipping Hara during the Hasta nakṣatra, one attains preeminence among one’s own kin;
the worshipper of Hara obtains a wife endowed with beauty, virtuous conduct, good qualities, and prosperity.
During the Citrā nakṣatra, the worshipper immediately gains these, and likewise during the Svātī asterism.
One will possess great wealth through trade, joined with abundant profit.
Having obtained [it], one dwells in happiness for a very long time;
having worshipped Śiva at Viśākhā, one attains many desired objects.
And for those performing [rites] under Anurādhā, they should give gifts in due order;
having worshipped Bhava under Jyeṣṭhā, one will certainly obtain wealth.
Under the Mūla asterism, the wise man, having worshipped Śiva, shall obtain health of body.
By worshipping Mahādeva during Pūrvāṣāḍhā, one attains fame. (3) During Uttarāṣāḍhā, the worshipper of Śambhu shall become a conqueror of enemies.
If there is worship of Hara during Śravaṇā, one shall obtain an excellent and auspicious maiden. (4)
If one worships Śiva under the Dhaniṣṭhā asterism, one obtains abundant and great wealth;
having acquired that wealth and enjoyed happiness, one should always be disposed toward giving.
When the deity Abhijit is sought, the worshipper who knows all matters attains the Veda together with its six limbs and the [divine] voice.
Under the Vāruṇa asterism, one should perform the worship of Śiva and obtain a physician and effective medicine;
under the asterism named Proṣṭhapadā, however, one should worship Śiva.
And by means of non-attachment, one frequently attains [liberation]; there is no doubt in this matter.
On the day of the Uttaraproṣṭhapadā constellation, the wise man should worship Śiva.
O twice-born ones, by the command of the Lord, there shall be liberation from all diseases.
For all men and women, [the worship of] Rāma is most excellent. (I.16a) Great anger at all times is destroyed by the worship of Śaṅkara.
That man who is a worshipper under the asterism Aśvinī shall obtain elephants and horses.
By worshipping Śiva under Bharaṇī, one obtains a long life;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform worship under these lunar mansions.
If one is unable to perform it oneself, the wise person should have others perform the propitiatory worship;
having done so, they will certainly obtain its fruit.
During the respective fixed lunar mansions, Śambhu should conduct the worship and the festival.
And one who observes a fast on the day of Ārdrā gains merit multiplied by ten million times that amount.
Even by performing worship, one may obtain sons and grandsons through this vow;
likewise, those who have received initiation—whether as a Samayin, a Putraka, or a Sādhaka—are pervaded [by its power].
He who does not observe the fast of Śarvakṣa shall go to the hell of sinners;
this applies to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even those who are kinsmen of the twice-born.
Whether she be a maiden, a widow, a woman of gentle mind, or one observing the vow of an ascetic,
she should perform this rite on every Śarva-day throughout all the months.
Having performed his bath at the time of twilight and having observed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā),
he should then perform the worship of Śiva, beginning with that of Svāyaṃbhuva and others;
and having conducted the worship up to the festival according to the prescribed rule, (7) [he should proceed].
Having circumambulated the Lord Śiva and praised him with the most excellent hymns, [he remained there].
Having prostrated many times with devotion... having reached his own home, he should feed [the guest].
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, however, in the presence of Rudra, Kṣetrapāla, and Śiva.
Having then made this resolve, the householder should observe it for one year;
whatever desire the practitioner longs for, that he shall obtain.
At the end of the year, the wise man should then perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*).
Having performed [the rites], he should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins according to his ability.
By that vow, one obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred million sacrifices, and the merit of giving away ten million maidens in marriage.
Through this [rite], his portents vanish, as do the terrible afflictions caused by enemies;
he becomes liberated from all diseases and endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth.
Having enjoyed great pleasures here, one prospers with long life and happiness.
This is the supreme secret, the most excellent among all vows.
(5) On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, at twilight, and on Mondays, [one should observe this].
Whatever fruit a man obtains by worshipping Hara on the occasion of a Vyatīpāta,
who could obtain that same fruit, that unsurpassed fruit of theirs—
even a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a killer of a cow, or one who violates the teacher’s bed?
One is liberated from the multitude of great sins by that supreme vow, [when given] to a devotee of Śiva who is peaceful, learned in the Vedas, and a householder. (7)
One should bestow this vow upon a poor person who is afflicted by a great disease.
Thus ends the ritual procedure beginning with the Bṛhattāla and ending with the Ṛkṣotsava, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara, in the *Kriyākramadyotikā*.
(2) Now follows the ritual procedure for expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is said to be the destruction [of a fault], while the mind is called the means of connection (*sandhāna*);
the reconnection of what has been lost is traditionally known as expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
By the omission of his own conduct, a human being goes to hell;
for the sake of purifying one whose conduct has been omitted, the Guru should prescribe an expiation.
When the beginning or end of a lunar day falls on a day afflicted by illness, there is fear of kings and thieves;
likewise, when it occurs during rites for teachers, fire, or deities, one incurs constant loss and misfortune.
Both the religious student (*brahmacārī*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*) have two types of penances prescribed for them;
these two are proclaimed to be of two kinds, according to whether the act was intentional (*sakāma*) or unintentional (*akāma*).
For an intentional act, the expiation is double that for an unintentional one. (5)
For a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), that [period] shall be double for one who subsists on alms.
For one dwelling in the forest, it consists of three qualities, while for ascetics, it consists of four;
this applies from after eighty years until before sixteen years [of age].

One should prescribe an expiation for that aged person and for a child; likewise, an expiation has been declared for women and for those who are ill. For one who is unable to perform it himself, however, the penance elsewhere is double.
For one who is incapable, [the funeral rites] should be performed by the son, brother, wife, and so forth, or by paternal kinsmen.
The penance must be performed in its entirety as explained in detail.
I shall now describe the procedure for the ritual bathing as proclaimed in the Śivasiddhānta.
That is declared to be threefold: the constant, the occasional, and the optional. Each one is said to be threefold: inferior, middling, and superior.
Subtracted by five and nine, there are twenty-five jars;
likewise, in the middle, there are forty-nine and eighty-one jars.
One hundred and eight is excellent; two hundred and sixteen is also praised;
five hundred and eight is called the middle; nine hundred is said to be the lowest.
The triad is considered, in order, to be the obligatory (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), and the optional (*kāmya*).
Austerity (*tapas*) is said to consist of the *kṛcchra* and other such penances; among these, the *kṛcchra* is designated as the "seven-heated" (*saptatapta*).
The *atikṛcchra* consists of two *parāka*s, followed by the procedure of the *candrāyaṇa*.
One should eat a single meal every third night and observe a fast for three days.
Thus the *kṛcchra* is fully described; it is known as the *prājāpatya*.
One should drink warm water for three days, followed by a diet of milk for three days.
When hot clarified butter is consumed for three days starting from the first day, and when it is taken alone for three days [subsequently],
that which is known as *Taptakṛcchra* is indeed described as a *Kṛcchra*.
Therein, consuming the milk of three fruits for twenty-one days is designated as *atikṛcchra*; now the *parāka* is described here:
fasting for twelve days is traditionally remembered as *parāka*.
There should be an increase of half a morsel per month during the bright fortnight, and one should decrease it during the dark fortnight.
In water prescribed by the rules for the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow, she becomes one whose essence is water.
(I.18a) As before, having prepared a circular sacrificial pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*) either in the pavilion or in its center,
and having placed four jars or four half-jars upon a heap of grain in the northwestern direction, (2)
Having performed the worship of Vighneśvara and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited,
one should worship Śivāstra in a single eastern jar preceded by the meditation (*dhyāna*) to be described hereafter;

and having worshipped [the deity] in a single southern jar preceded by the meditation on Aghora as previously stated— or alternatively, [worship] Aghorāstra according to what will be described hereafter.

Having worshipped the Pāśupatāstra in the western jar according to what will be described later, one should worship Pratyaṅgirā herself in the northern jar (4). Those initiated into the five directions should recite the *Kāmika* and other Śiva-jñāna scriptures, which have arisen facing their respective directions, an infinite number of times in the five directions (5); they should mutter the Tatpuruṣa and other mantras an infinite number of times in the eastern and other directions.

They should perform the study of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures, as well as the recitation of the *Śānti* hymns, and chant [the mantra] an infinite number of times as prescribed for the consecration pavilion (*pratiṣṭhā-maṇḍapa*).

(6) Having worshipped these [deities] in sequence up to the end of the chanting, immediately thereafter, in the central sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should perform the ritual actions—beginning with the purification of the pit and ending with the expiatory oblation of the *caru*—as previously described; then, having worshipped each individual form (*mūrti*) in order, (7)

One should perform the oblation (*juhuyāt*). Alternatively, in four sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), they should invoke the respective deities along with the presiding forms (*mūrtīpa*) and offer oblations.

(I.18b) They should offer honey-triad, the three sweets, sesame, *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), milk, or *kusara* porridge, along with the three pungents (*kaṭatraya*), the three fruits, and mustard seeds—either one hundred, one thousand, or half that number—daily at dawn and dusk, accompanied by the *pūrṇāhuti*, ending with "svāhā. (2)

"O Blessed One, please again perform the curse for all those who cause agitation. Reciting this together with the mantra ten times constitutes another stage of the practice. In the case of many days or fortnights, having restrained the *śiva* right there, one should go into the presence of the deity, announce the performance of the *homa*, establish protection, and pray for the destruction of misfortune.
May there be peace through the unbroken flow of one, five, seven, nine, ten, twelve, twenty-one, and all the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*s).
Thus, peace.
Now follows the propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma).

As before, having placed a single water-pot (kuṃbha) adorned with all ornaments upon a heap of all kinds of grain on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) within the pavilion, and having arranged eight smaller pots around it, one should worship the firm seat (sthirāsana) in the central pot and meditate upon the Pāśupata weapon (astra).
Seated upon the throne of the *praṇava*, invincible, and possessed of great strength;
five-faced, ten-eared, with three eyes in every countenance;
fierce with fangs that are formidable, emitting a roar, and difficult to conquer. (7)
Wearing a garland of skulls and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
With squinting eyes, adorned with great serpents, and licking his fangs with laughter;

possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, he is the crusher of the hosts of obstructors. Endowed with ten most fierce arms and terrible weapons, he holds in his right hands a sword, a bow, a great trident, and a noose that grants fearlessness.
In his left hands, he holds a shield, a skull-bowl, and an excellent spear;
he is endowed with reddish-brown beard and eyebrows, as well as hair of the same color.
One should meditate upon the Great Lord, who bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
Having meditated thus,
one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation and ending with the worship of the requisites for enjoyment— such as *oṃ ślīṃ kārasamāyuktaṃ paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṇṇamasvāhā*—
in the vases starting from the east, and having worshipped the vajra and other implements as before.

Having offered various food offerings (*naivedya*) and the like, and having performed the dedication of the recitation (*japa*), one should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and sit down.

(5) Having completed the consecration of the pit and the rites up to the oblation of the *caru* and the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*), one should worship the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) in its center as before—[offering] sacrificial wood (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sesame seeds (*tila*), parched grain flour (*sattu*), *dūrvā* grass, the three sweets (*madhutraya*), the three honeys (*madhuratrāya*), and the three fruits (*phalatraya*). For the removal of those respective defects, one should offer oblations ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*—either one hundred, a thousand, or one hundred and eight times—with that specific mantra; having offered until the end of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and concluding with the *pūrṇāhuti*, and having presented incense and lamps, one should consign the fire into the pitcher (*kumbha*), and consecrate the deity with the waters contained within that pitcher. (I.19b)

Having performed the recitation of the *Kāmika* and other scriptures, as well as the recitation for pacification (*śānti*), according to the number of days prescribed for the "many-day" (*bahudivasa*) rite, and having fed the Brahmins as before, one should conclude.

Regarding the other auxiliary rite for atonement, which is the ritual bathing (*snāna*): having installed the *liṅga*, the *bherī*, the *ghaṭī*, and so forth upon the altar in the center of the previously described pavilion, and having placed the *Śivāstra* in front of that in one jar and eight jars around it—one should worship the *Śivāstra* in the central jar, which is endowed with all splendor. (4)
Having prepared the seat as before,
[one should visualize] the four-faced one with blazing kuśa grass, possessing a radiance like a mass of lightning,
with a head adorned by the moon, and having four sprout-like hands.
[He is] like a thunderbolt joined with fire, unbearable and of terrible prowess;
endowed with twelve eyes, and bearing the [mudrās of] power, the trident, fearlessness, and the boon;
the crusher of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and wicked rākṣasas. (6)
I bow to the divine Śivāstra, which has blood-red eyes and is most terrible.

Having meditated thus, having worshipped with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), and having prepared [the materials] in either a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should offer the oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) therein, satisfy [the deity] up to the point of the expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), and then make known the petition for one's desired object.

Alternatively, [one should place] the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī* in the eastern direction; the *śivāstra* in the south; the *aghorāstra* in the west; and the *pāśupatāstra* in the north, which they call the *pratyaṅgirasa*.
Oṃ hrīṃ kāraṃ, then the word "kṛṣṇavāsase," (2) and then "siṃhavadane" and also "mahāvadane."

Then [one should utter] "Mahābhairavī," followed by all the syllables, and at the end of that, "Karmavidhvaṃsanī. Then follows the supreme mantra-word; thereafter, one should extract "Chedinī" and also "Sarvabhūtadamanī."
One should extract the word "bandha" (bind) from the end of all beings.
Sever the state of all obstacles; that which is the word "sever the obstacles" (vighnacindhī), and sever all diseases; that which is the word "sever" (nikṛnta).
In the subsequent [mantra], there are the words "O you who devour all wicked beings from every side, devour!
(5), followed again by the words for the contraction of the mouth: "O you with flaming tongues, O terrible one! (vaktrasaṃṣṭrapada).

In the *pratyaṅgira* [mantra], one should extract the word "paścāt" followed by "namaḥ" and the word "svāhā"; this is the mantra consisting of the *pratyaṅgira*. Having worshipped the Supreme Goddess *pratyaṅgira* upon a firm seat in the center of the *sarvaśobhanavāra*, one should meditate [on her] as having the face of a lion, fierce fangs, and a crest of flames with upward-pointing rays.
She was endowed with three red eyes that were round and resembled black collyrium.
Carrying in her two left hands a trident and a hand-drum,
and carrying in her two left hands a severed head and a sprout.
Wearing black garments, with tearful eyes and a face emaciated by flesh, she was intent on dancing;
her every limb was adorned with suitable ornaments of pearls.
(2) She was possessed of a delight in loud laughter and was equipped with a black sword.
In meditation, I am Pratyangirā, the destroyer of diseases, obstacles, and enemies.

Having meditated thus, one should perform the invocation and other rites with all the offerings (*upacāra*) using that [mantra] as the root; thereafter, having worshipped up to the end of the worship of the enclosure jars (*āvaraṇakalaśa*), one should worship Pratyaṅgirā in the middle of a lotus-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) or in a womb-shaped pit (*yonikuṇḍa*). Then, with fuel-sticks of *plakṣa* and other trees, products of the cow (*gavya*), sesame, *dūrvā* grass, milk-rice (*caru*), the three sweets (*madhutraya*), the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), *gāra*, mustard seeds, cloves (*lavaṅga*), nutmeg leaves (*jātipatra*), and *śrīgandha*— (5) [The text continues here.]

One should offer oblations one hundred, one hundred, fifty, or twenty-eight times for each of these substances, such as saffron (*kuṅkuma*) and yellow orpiment (*gorocanā*). (6) Having performed the expiation and offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and having prayed to the Goddess for the pacification of those misdeeds, one should cause [the person] to be bathed with that water from the jar, which has been poured out among the deities... (7)
Alternatively, as before, one should worship the four weapons and Pratyaṅgirā in the center; thus they say—this is the homa according to the directions.

The *saṃhitā-homa* (I.21a) is performed as follows: having fully worshipped Śiva, together with the *brahmāṅga* [mantras] and his attendants, either in the perpetual fire (*nityāgni*) or in another fire, for the removal of those defects, one should offer oblations—such as fuel sticks (*samidh*) and other materials—with the *brahmāṅga* mantras, a hundred, a thousand, or half that number.
One should then perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth. This is the *saṃhitā-homa*, described as "enclosed within a jar" (*ghaṭavargita*).
The Ritual for the Homa of the Mūrti—
Now follows the ritual for the homa of the mūrti.

On the roof of a palace, or elsewhere on a prepared sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the center of a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), one should place the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī*, as well as the eight jars designated as the *vajra* and so forth in the eight directions—these being provided with cords and lids, and filled with cloth, gold, gems, medicinal herbs, and scented water.

Having performed the purification of the pavilion and other preliminary rites as before, one should worship Śiva in the central [jar] and worship the Aghora weapon in the *vardhanī*. Alternatively, one may place the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī* in the center.
Having established [the deity] therein, one should worship the Aghora weapon (*aghorāstra*).

One should worship the Vajra and other [weapons] surrounding that. (6) "Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ to the seat of the weapon (*astrāsana*); huṃ phaṭ namaḥ to the form of the weapon (*astramūrti*). Having worshipped thus, one should meditate [on the deity] as having the brilliance of a thousand suns and a voice like the rumbling of a dense cloud. (7)
His neck and face were illuminated by the tips of his blazing fangs.
Three-eyed, with the tongue of a woman, possessing blazing eyebrows, beard, and hair on his head,
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, and bearing a trident, sword, spear,
and mallet; four-armed, four-faced, with the crescent of the autumn moon as his crest-ornament.
He was dancing, possessed of a massive body, and adorned with ornaments of serpents.
"The crushing of the arrogant gods, dānavas, and daityas.
Having thus meditated.
The word *oṃ sphura sphura*, followed by the pair *prasphurat*;
the word *tanurūpa*, followed by the word *caṭa caṭa*;
then the pair *pracaṭat*, followed by the word *kahakaha*. (3)

"Vama vama," "bandha" twice, then "ghātaya" twice; this is declared as the Aghora weapon mantra, ending with "huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having thus known the mantra, one should worship, [beginning] from the invocation up to the recitation (*japa*). Having worshipped in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should invoke the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) along with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*ājya*).

For the purpose of removing that defect, one should offer oblations— one hundred, one thousand, fifty, or one hundred and eight times each— of sesame seeds, milk, dūrvā grass, the three sweets, and sacrificial food (haviṣya), using the Aghorāstra mantra,
accompanied by the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Alternatively, having placed the Śiva-pitcher in the center and the Vardhanī pitcher [beside it], one should worship the eight deities beginning with Śarva in the eight directions; or, according to the five-fold system, one should worship the forms beginning with Earth.

...having performed the oblations up to the end of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should offer one hundred and eight or fifty oblations for each of the following— palāśa, udumbara, aśvattha, vaṭa, śamī, khadira, āyu, āplakṣa, and so forth— separately with their respective mantras. Having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should sprinkle the linga, the image (*bera*), or the patron (*yajamāna*) with that water, apply the ashes, and perform everything according to the number of days prescribed for the rite of pacification (*śānti*).

In this regard, after the *Ayana-śānti* has been recited, the patron (*yajamāna*), having adorned the readers of the *Kāmika-tantra* and other scriptures with hymns, perfumes, flowers, garments, and so forth, led by the preceptor (*ācārya*), shall give the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (4) Having prostrated, he should pray for the pacification of misfortunes. Together with his parents, the preceptor should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). One should satisfy the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the helpless with food and clothing. This concludes the *Mūrti-homa*. (5–6)
Having touched one who has been initiated into his own caste, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
upon touching a Śūdra, one should immediately perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Upon touching any of the intermediate spaces, one should perform two ritual baths.
At the time of seeing a Cāṇḍāla, one should always remember Sadāśiva;
having heard his speech, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
If one should touch [the object] merely by the staff, two baths must be performed.
(I.22b) In the event of accidental contact, one should know that first there is a bath of water;
having then performed a bath of ashes, one should mutter the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
If, however, the contact occurs intentionally, one should perform twice the previous penance.
Upon seeing him at the time of a meal, a wise man should not discard the remaining food.
Then, having performed the two ablutions and recited the root mantra eight hundred times,
any foul odor present at the tip of the nose shall be carried away by the wind.

Having accepted cow dung, one should immediately conquer the five-syllable mantra. Having eaten the food of those who have not been initiated according to their own caste, or while staying in a new house in a village, one should recite the *Vyomavyāpin* once; if one so desires, one may recite it a hundred times.
O Brahmins, upon eating the food of a king, one should recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times.
Having eaten even the food of a Vaiśya, one should gradually recite it up to a thousand times.
Having eaten the food of a Śūdra out of desire, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances. (5–6)
One who eats out of desire should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, as well as the Kṛcchra and the Atikṛcchra; indeed, after eating for three days, one should perform the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa.
...due to being constantly [associated with them], the status of an Indra is attained. (7) But one who is joined with a Śūdra should always behave like a Śūdra.
Having had sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman, one should then perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance;
for [intercourse] with a woman of the class immediately above [one's own], the *taptakṛcchra* and the month-long [penance] should be observed.
For six months or even for a year, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
however, beyond a year, if the union has occurred, no atonement is prescribed.
(2) His conduct should likewise be such, especially until death.
If one should feed [them] in vessels made of castor-seed wood, arka, vaṭa, or aśvattha;
Whether out of desire or even without desire, one should mutter the Śiva-mantra a hundred times while [consuming] food that is mixed with ghee,
accompanied by milk, and devoid of salt.
Having recited the *Ajāhṛdaya* mantra, which cuts through all defects—
even upon seeing hair, bones, nails, insects, or the like—
one should discard a small amount of food, wash one's hands, and [apply] ash. (4)
O Lord of Gods, by touching [the image], remembering [the deity], and drinking water, one becomes purified.
One should avoid garlic, fish, meat, and the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
If, however, one has consumed these through negligence, one should recite the Śiva-mantra while remaining pure.
If one should eat out of desire, one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times;
[this applies even for] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, or the theft of gold.

Approaching the wife of one's guru constitutes the fifth [heinous act]; through association with these, they become the five [sins]. Violation of the guru’s bed, drinking liquor, and the killing of a Brahmin—these are declared to be acts ending in death; now hear of their atonement through death.
One who steals silver out of greed should observe the lunar vow (*cāndrāyaṇa*). For stealing more than ten *gadyāṇas*, one should perform twice that penance;
for stealing up to a thousand, however, the rule for gold is prescribed.
For stealing the finest gems, one should perform the penance prescribed for the theft of gold;
for all other minerals and metals, however, one should perform the Parāka penance.
For the theft of grains, a *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed; for sesame seeds, an *aiḍava* is traditionally taught.
For the theft of base metals and gems, a *ghora-kṛcchra* lasting two thousand [verses] is ordained.
For the theft of garments, bedding, seats, and the like, one thousand repetitions of the *gāyatrī* are required.
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for fifty thousand repetitions of this, which is equal to violating the teacher’s bed.
(4) The killing of a cow, being a Vratya, earning wealth through the profession of arms, failing to maintain the sacred fires, and marrying before one's elder brother—these are [offenses]. (5)
Killing a woman, a deer, or a kṣatriya; subsisting on forbidden things;
nihilism; the violation of vows; and the sale of one's own daughters.
Dealing in grain, officiating at sacrifices for those who tend cattle, and officiating at sacrifices for others; the sale of one's father, mother, or friends; the sale of tanks and groves;
(7) the sale of a maiden, the marrying of a younger sister before the elder, and officiating at sacrifices for such persons.
For a maiden, crookedness and the breaking of her vow [are grounds for loss].
The rites of establishing the sacred fires, marriage, and sexual intercourse;
the abandonment of Vedic study, the abandonment of one's son, and the abandonment of one's kinsmen. (I.24a)
Seeking firewood, cutting down trees, harming rice crops, living by medicine, using harmful mantras, [selling] places of refuge, engaging in vices, selling oneself,
(2) associating with wicked teachers, and holding authority over those who appear [deceitful].
And the sale of what should not be sold—each of these is likewise a minor offense (upapātaka).
Purification for minor offenses may be achieved through the Aindava vow,
by subsisting on milk for a month, or by the Parāka penance.
Furthermore, a specific distinction regarding the Aghora [rite] is now proclaimed:
one should perform a fourth part of the penance for killing a Brahmin when killing a Kṣatriya;
(4) one should perform an eighth part when killing a Vaiśya, and a sixteenth part for a Śūdra.

Likewise, for the killing of living beings, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times. By reciting the Aghora mantra a hundred times, one is purified from the sin consisting of the injury of living beings;
this applies when one kills boneless creatures or those born from sweat. (5–6)
For one who unintentionally kills a hundred animals of the same species, the penance is half of that;
for one who destroys fire, flowers, and the like, or even many bones, [the penance is likewise reduced].
Having seen both desirable and undesirable things, one becomes pure by remembering Śiva;
even for the killing of a mouse or a cat, one becomes pure by [that] very hundred-fold [remembrance]. (7)

In the case of killing a dog or a jackal, the penance is double; for killing a monkey or a cock, it is likewise double. For all [other] animals, such as the *andhaja* and *yāta*, and even among birds such as the swan (*haṃsa*) and so forth, [the penance is double].
However, for killing a lion and other such beasts, or for killing goats and other such livestock, [the penance is double].

By reciting the *Bahurūpa* mantra one hundred and four times, one becomes pure after killing a hundred animals. Having killed a cow through negligence, one becomes pure by reciting the *Ghoralakṣa* mantra one hundred thousand times.
Having committed the murder of a woman or a child, one is purified by the *Ghoralakṣa* mantra.
Having cut off the nose or other [limbs] of anyone, a wise man should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
likewise, for one who intentionally causes an abortion, he should recite it ten thousand times.
Even one bitten by a dog shall be purified by reciting the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times;
one bitten by a cat or a mouse is purified by reciting it one hundred times.
One bitten by a jackal, a wolf, or a dog is purified by [the recitation of] one hundred and eight [times];
however, one bitten by a crocodile or a makara is purified by [reciting it] only once.
If one should [bite] a serpent through negligence, one should mutter the *ghora-sahasra* [mantra] one thousand times.
One should recite the mantra prescribed for Pārśva and the others ten thousand times; one should also recite the Ghorā mantra ten thousand times.
If they should practice the science of poisons... [it would become] unstable.
For Bhūtas, Grahas, Piśācas, and so forth, [one should recite] two hundred times.
One should perform the killing through the mind alone;
having performed expulsion and so forth, one should do so with the *Bahurūpāyuta* mantra.
One who lives by inflicting suffering upon others through physical actions...
having fully understood [this], one should recite the auspicious mantra a hundred times.
He who speaks untruth through action, mind, or speech...
By reciting the Vāmadeva hymn one hundred times, one shall be released from that sin.
It is said that for a hundred [repetitions] regarding what is undesirable, one should recite twice as many for verbal faults;
likewise for the mental resolve toward another's wife or property and the contemplation of what is undesirable.
And the fourth mental action is the insistence on what should not be done;
(3) it consists of idle chatter day and night, as well as that which is untrue and unpleasant.
Slandering others is the fourth verbal action;
eating what is unfit to be eaten, violence, and indulgence in false desires [are the other three].
(4) Taking the property of others is the fourth bodily action.
For the vocal [karma], I shall practice silence, fire-rituals, worship, and recitation.
(5) When these are completed, one should offer them to the Guru, the Deity, or others.
Thus liberated from the bonds of speech and the bonds of karma... (6)
By fasting for three nights, bathing in water at the three junctions of the day,
chanting the Brahma-mantra, and observing silence, one is not released from the bonds of karma.
When one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) have been performed,
one is liberated from mental sin by means of the Śivagāyatrī mantra.
Having recited the mantra ten thousand times for the removal of all defects, the practitioner,
by drinking the five products of the cow once, is liberated from all sins. Whatever [sin] has arisen from mother or father, whether innate or adventitious—
Sin that has reached the very marrow of the bones is consumed in an instant by the five products of the cow.
If semen or similar fluids should flow while one is sleeping unintentionally,
one should bathe again with one's clothes on and recite the Astra-mantra one hundred times.
If this occurs during the day or in a dream while riding a vehicle, one should perform the rite twice as many times.

Having united with a woman out of desire, one should rotate the *praṇava* of the Great Soul a hundred thousand times by means of the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇāvarti-nirodha*). (3) This is the injunction.
An ascetic who is attached to sense objects, placing an old woman at the forefront, may take a wife;
otherwise, his downfall is certain.
[He should maintain] matted hair, a tuft of hair, and so forth on the body, as well as ashes... [and other signs].
For as long as one might dwell among women, for that much time shall the fool reside in the most terrible Raurava hell.
O Vāmadeva, by means of a thousand [recitations], one is purified; of this there is no doubt.
But by forcefully abandoning the white [path], one is purified in four hundred days.
At night, one should recite it seven hundred times; during the day, one should recite it seven hundred times.
When one sees animal play involuntarily, one should recite it one hundred times.
When the wife has bathed after her menses, then for a period of five days—
One should serve one's wife for the sake of obtaining sons; otherwise, one becomes a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā).
Then, having emerged from the ascetic state, one should perform recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth;
for he who, deluded by desire, constantly engages in sexual intercourse over a long period, [is lost].
One who possesses wisdom should be known as being like a donkey; those who are averse to his mantra [are likewise].

There is no fault in [approaching] a Kṣatriya woman and others, but one incurs fault by doing so during the day or on a sacred festival day. In deed, thought, or speech, one must never commit adultery.

If one should, out of delusion, perform [sexual intercourse] during the period of purification according to the half-verse injunction, it must be performed with double the penance in the case of a maiden, and likewise among other castes. Sexual intercourse on the junctions of lunar phases, on the eighth day, or ever by day [is forbidden].
The wise one, established in the enclosure, should recite the *praṇava* ten thousand times;
having performed half of that at night, he should recite it ten thousand times during the twilight.
Having heard a story concerning sexual intercourse, one whose seed has been lost should recite the *śata* [of the Gāyatrī] a hundred times;
having fallen from celibacy, the wise man should perform the prescribed penance.
One should recite ten thousand times for a common woman; for a Śūdra woman, double that amount.
Having heard [the mantra] from one born of any caste for the purpose of subjugation and so forth, one should recite it forty thousand times.
This burns away the sins of the womb, as well as whatever else may exist.

Furthermore, one who desires Kāmārī, the upholder of the great vow, should— being purified by a thousand recitations— especially recite [the mantra] a hundred times if he is a householder who has committed the act of approaching a woman who should not be approached, even if her nose and lips have been severed. (7)
If one who has been initiated should approach a Brahmin woman or any other [woman],
the Brāhmaṇa is freed from that sin by reciting [the sacred syllable] one hundred and eight times.
A Kṣatriya is not purified by two hundred [recitations], nor indeed a Vaiśya by three hundred;
a Śūdra, however, having recited it one hundred times, becomes like Maheśvara himself, O elder brother of Śiva.
Having remained for one night in fasting, he is liberated from that sin.
Having eaten as much as desired, one should perform a kṛcchra penance for every hundred [mouthfuls] of those [forbidden things].
Having approached out of delusion a woman who is discolored, or one who is of that nature and acts according to her lust,
he shall remain for three days without anxiety, standing in water reaching up to his navel.
By means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite [the mantra]; thus one is purified from secret sins.
(4) Having gone to the water, one should perform the ritual of clothing and observe a fast.
Whatever must be done by the Guru should indeed be performed out of desire; however, if a Caṇḍāla woman, through ignorance, is present in the temple—
One should abandon earthen [objects]...
having bathed immediately, that house is purified...
(6) Having recited the *Narāyaṇa* [hymn] five thousand times, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance.
Having eaten [the food], one who desires to begin the evening [rite] should first perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Having recited the Vāmadeva hymn ten thousand times, one is purified by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
(7) If it has been consumed intentionally, then [one should perform] the Kṛcchra and other such penances.
In the same way, one should mutter the Vāmadeva [mantra] when another's beloved is present; this is considered the vow.
Having known her to have been enjoyed for a long time, he then becomes equal to her.
(I.27a) Having touched a washerwoman, a female laborer, or one staying in the temple...
By abandoning the merchandise, there is purification from the goat; for three days, five thousand [coins].
Having unintentionally touched or eaten [impure things], one should mutter the *ghora* mantra for three days;
if done intentionally, it must be performed twice as long, otherwise one is not purified at all.
If a practice lasting many days has arisen out of desire,
then one should perform it once through that single conjunction.

If a long period of association occurred unintentionally for both of them, then the Cāndrāyaṇa penance must be performed; otherwise, purification is not attained. (4) If a long-term association occurred intentionally...
In that case, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance must be performed, and not merely the Vāruṇa offerings.

One who accepts improper gifts is freed from that sin immediately by performing the Dvādaśa sacrifice again; likewise, one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice is quickly liberated, provided he does not revile [the officiant].
Having taken ghee, oil, and sugar, one should practice on the left [nostril];
likewise, salt, ginger, pungent substances, and various perfumes.
Milk, curd, ghee, oil, honey, meat, coriander, silk cloth, cotton, silence, honeycomb, and a grass mat—
having gone to a place where leather is sold, one should mutter the *ghora* mantra three hundred times.
A collection of metals such as gold, and a multitude of gems such as diamonds.
Minerals such as yellow orpiment, collections of other precious substances,
a bull, an elephant, a vehicle, a field, and likewise the intermediate space.

One becomes pure by making an effort regarding the *ālaya* and other [impurities], and by removing hundreds of various forms [of defilement] from wood, stones, leaves, and so forth. A man [is purified] from fear, women, or even a hundred or a thousand [such things] that flow incessantly. (2)
One should perform one thousand circumambulations of the house while holding abundant grain.
Having taken up some object as if it were a material thing, the wise man should mutter [the mantra] many times;
for the theft of clothing, bedding, seats, and so forth, one hundred recitations of the Gāyatrī are required.
A wise person should recite the mantra one thousand times for the removal of the power of knowledge (vidyā-tāpa).
He who, having abandoned his wife, speaks otherwise, or he who behaves toward her differently—
such a person, though initiated for the sacrifice, has fallen from his status and must undergo initiation again.

By constantly reciting the Aghora mantra for one month before Śiva and offering ten thousand oblations into the Śiva-fire, one is liberated from that sin. One should repeat the Aghora mantra ten times when crossing a triple or quadruple junction.
Even when a multitude of sins has arisen through their confluence,
the Aghora mantra should be recited until the mind becomes serene.
He who studies the Śiva-saṃhitā day after day according to the prescribed rule—
He destroys all sins as the sun dispels the darkness;
having joined the morning and evening sessions, he should recite the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times.
Sin committed during a day and night perishes at that very moment.
When a woman who has reached her menses is not yet purified, she should worship Śiva.
On the first day she is a Cāṇḍālī; on the second, a slayer of a Brahmin.
In the third [watch] she is called a washerwoman; in the fourth, she becomes pure through bathing.
Having performed the bath with clay and consumed the products of the cow (*gavya*), one should worship Śiva.
(2) In the absence of the *aghora* mantra, one should worship Śiva after reciting it a hundred times.

Alternatively, the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) or meditation (*dhyāna*) should be performed during the first three days. If there is dust on the day [of the festival], then the first day is at night, excluding the third part of the day;
if it occurs in the morning during the third part, then the first day is desired here.
If the flow of menses is not noticed, she becomes impure like one who has had sexual intercourse within her own home.
An object that has been touched or seen is not defiled by mere proximity [to the following]:
a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse, a dog, or one who is in a state of ritual impurity due to a death.
Upon hearing of the death of a relative who has been touched [by an impurity], one should perform a *prājāpatya* penance after bathing in a river or similar body of water,
or after eating; or,
if a Brāhmaṇa woman touches a Śūdra woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Kṣatriya woman while they are weeping, [she too must perform this penance].
One becomes purified by performing the *kṛcchra* penance for three-quarters or half [of its duration], respectively. (6) If one eats without having bathed, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow.
[This applies to those who have touched] jackals, dogs, donkeys, and the like, as well as insects, outcasts, and those of the lowest castes.
If one touches animals without having bathed, one should perform an *atikṛcchra* penance;
for [touching] a Śūdra and others, purification is achieved through gifts and fasts consisting of quarter-*kṛcchras*.

Having touched a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or a woman of the twice-born castes, one becomes pure by performing a quarter-kṛcchra penance; upon touching a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Śūdra woman, one is purified by a pāda-kṛcchra.

Having touched a woman previously married to a Śūdra, one is purified by giving a gift alone. But having touched a menstruating woman who is eating out of delusion, or one who has been touched by corpses and the like,
one should perform a Kṛcchra penance after three days have passed, or a Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If one should touch food being eaten by a menstruating woman or by a person of ill repute,

one should observe three days of fasting and is purified by the *pañcagavya*. If a *caṇḍāla* enters while one is eating and has not yet rinsed one's mouth after finishing the meal, [one must likewise fast].

If one eats before bathing after a fast, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (4) If a person of the same lineage (*sagotra*) who is menstruating is touched, one should likewise fast for three days.

Having touched a woman in her courses who has been touched by another such woman, one becomes pure by bathing and sprinkling oneself with water. Likewise, one becomes pure after conversing with her; but having seen a menstruating woman, one is purified only after eating.
One should not eat at the wrong time nor go near the fire; thereafter, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Even while a period of impurity due to death or birth is occurring, if menstruation should take place, [one must likewise perform this purification].
Having bathed, one should eat; and having eaten, one should fast for the day.

If there should be impurity due to a corpse, impurity from water-contact, or birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), one may eat after sprinkling oneself in the midst [of the rite]; but if one is touched by what has been left over from eating, a *kṛcchra* penance is required. (7)
Having eaten or drunk while a woman is menstruating or has recently given birth, one has likewise acted [in this manner].
If a woman in her courses has sexual intercourse when she has become impure, purification occurs through a ceremonial bath; otherwise, there shall be fasting for three days.
One should bathe with clay and water from a well that has been drawn up while it is still impure;
one should bathe in the morning on the fourth day, at the conclusion of six nāḍīs.
The purification of a vessel that has not been smeared [with impurities] is by means of heating with alkaline substances (*ūṣa*), steaming (*utsvedana*), or fragments of clay (*khaṇḍa*) and so forth;
for a bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsya*), it is purified by fire after being smeared with ashes twenty-one times.
One should wash a bed with water; if it is not smeared [with impurities], it is purified by washing it at that very moment.

She is purified by crossing over a cow's footprint in regions where [otherwise] she would have been defiled. (4) If, having bathed after her menses, she should out of force or delusion look upon others while separated from her husband, or if she should go with a paramour to a place where there is neither grass nor water, (5) [she is purified by the aforementioned penance].
The bath is prescribed there before the cow-hair fan;
the cow-hair fan is a whisk, or else it is a staff measuring one man's height.
If there is an obstruction by grass or leaves, or if it is separated by a substance, or even by a cow-tail fan, no bathing is required in that case. (6)
Having seen [the deity] established in the midst of the ritual action, one should mutter the *praṇava* of the householder.
After that, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), there is the vision of the Sun.
(7) Others also, having performed the vision, should mutter the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) one hundred times.

A Caṇḍāla who has climbed onto the same tree as [a Brahmin], or a woman in her courses— having stayed [there] for one night, he becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). For women, purification is prescribed to last until the twelfth day, like that for urine.
The bath should take place after eighteen days; beyond that, she remains impure for three nights. As for a woman who has become menstruating again while still in her previous menstrual flow:
After twenty days have passed, she shall remain impure for three nights.
Having touched her teeth and other such things, she should repeatedly cleanse the impurity with earth and bathe.
Then, having consumed the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) or clarified butter, she should worship Śiva.
One should perform the internal sacrifice oneself in the three directions starting from the east;
or else, at the end, one should recite the *ghora-mantra* a thousand times. Having touched [the object] with the mudrā of one's own caste, if one desires [a result], one should worship Śiva.
Then one should recite the mantra of the Lord of one's own lineage one thousand times;
even if performed through ignorance, one becomes pure through that ancillary rite.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times when a doubt has arisen;
in the case of contact with those of low birth, the recitation should be two, three, or four times that number respectively.
(6) Upon contact with those of superior birth, one of lower birth should perform half of that [recitation].
During the period of impurity caused by birth or death, one should perform meditation on the Lord according to one's ability.
At the end of that, having bathed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, being unwearied in mind toward Śiva,
one should recite the *Ghoratara-śata* one hundred times after bathing, having touched a human bone still moist with fat.
Upon touching one who is unanointed with oil, one should bathe or show [the water] while remaining silent.
One who has touched a corpse or one who handles the dead... (I.30a) ...should bathe after touching those who carry or burn [the corpse], as well as those who bear other sectarian marks.

Having performed his bath with those who follow the Pāñcarātra, Kālarātra, Sparśa, Kāpālika, Ālika, Bakāśa, Somabhūti, the Buddhists, the naked ones, and the black-robed ones, he becomes, while still clothed, one whose splendor is a hundred times that of the third [sun].
Upon the fourth touch, a Brahmin should perform a bath without his clothes;
having touched all the intermediate spaces, he should perform two baths.
One should perform a bath within five or six *daṇḍas* of a blacksmith during the *yugādi* festivals;
