likewise, one should bathe within two *daṇḍas* of a butcher or a washerman.
One should bathe within one and a half *daṇḍas* of women who are in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
Likewise, upon touching a crow, a vulture, a donkey, a horse, or an outcaste,
as well as those with deformed limbs, a corpse, a limb of a funeral pyre, village pigs, or cocks,
or upon touching discarded flower offerings, those who eat such remnants, or a fallen person, one should perform a ritual bath.
Upon contact with a jackal, a chameleon, a bat, a crow,
or an outcaste dog-cooker, one should perform a purificatory bath according to Varuṇa.
Having touched a Divākīrti, a Citrapūpa, a Niṣāda, a woman who has recently given birth, a twice-born man who follows forbidden occupations, or a Lokāyatika nihilist;
Likewise, having touched a sacred tree (*caityavṛkṣa*), one should enter the water with one's clothes on;
and if a Brāhmaṇa should happen to dwell there while mounted upon a single bull, or if a Caṇḍāla or similar person should be present, he attains purity through bathing.

Upon contact with semen or urine, one should bathe, except when the hands are above them; likewise after vomiting or purging. One should perform a bath upon touching those parts that are above the navel, for they are pure in every respect.
Those things which are otherwise pure become impure through contact with the body and its excretions; when the body has become impure, it is purified by seven applications of clay.

In the event of an injury to the head, one should perform a bath with water. Upon being touched by a dog or other such animals, or by birds such as crows and the like, one becomes pure by performing purification with clay on the first part [of the body].
(4) If purification has not been performed, one becomes pure by applying clay to the first part.
In all cases involving the head, one should indeed perform a bath with water.

A wise man should perform the expiation by reciting the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times, after he has performed the purification according to the rules following the smearing of food-leavings. (5–6)
Having bathed, one attains purity there through three hundred and ten-fold [repetition];
however, for speaking falsehood or passing urine, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
The face should not be touched by one who has discharged semen, urine, or feces;
it becomes pure by wiping it with clay and cow dung and then rinsing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having touched human bone, fat, excrement, menstrual blood, urine, semen, marrow, or blood, one should perform a full bath after overturning [the vessel].
... Having touched water [in such a case], one becomes pure by performing a bath.
If one is touched by such a person while still impure from food remnants, one becomes purified only by bathing.
Bathing during the day, when joined with the rays of the sun, is... (2) But that is not recommended at night, except for the appearance of the sun.
Alternatively, at night, one should perform a bath according to the instructions of the guru and others;
a householder should always perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) and the mantra-bath (*mantrasnāna*).
If another person of the same caste should touch one who is impure, that person becomes defiled.
If one who has touched that [food] is touched by another who is defiled, this same rule applies to all cases of being rendered impure by leavings.
During divine processions, weddings, sacrifices that have been commenced,
and at all festive celebrations, food touched by those who are themselves touched does not become defiled.
At a sacred ford, at a wedding, on a pilgrimage, in battle, during a national upheaval,
and in the event of a city or village fire, one does not incur fault by touching those who should not be touched.

The drops that fall from a Brahmin while he is not making himself impure by food-leavings do not lead him to sin; nor do those that pass over his beard or enter the spaces between his teeth. This applies also in the case of the *madhuparka*, the *soma* sacrifice, and when offering the *prāṇāhuti* oblations into water.
There is no impurity for one who has not left food remnants [in the mouth], nor for those two [the teacher and the disciple] when hair is involved.
Even when betel has been eaten, it is especially so;
upon touching what is stuck between the teeth, a man does not become impure by leaving food remnants.
With these leaves, roots, and flowers, as well as with those made of grass,
wood, and fragrant substances, a twice-born man does not become impure by eating the remnants.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked along a road;
after sipping water and then sipping again, and also after putting on a garment; having voided urine or excrement, one who has not yet sipped water should touch water.
One becomes pure after touching impure bodily excretions.
[Purification is prescribed] upon sneezing, spitting, speaking untruth, or hearing [the mention of] falsehood;
likewise after spitting, after anointing the body, and even after eating and putting on [clothes].
Likewise, from touching those who have food remnants [on them], or from the water used for washing feet;
from conversing with one who has food remnants [on them], and until the removal of that impurity.

One should always perform the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśet*) even without the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), as well as upon touching a desired object such as a *liṅga*, or upon seeing those dressed in other [inauspicious] garments;
and likewise, having touched something stuck to the teeth, one should sip water after touching the tongue. (5)
Having crossed water, one should sip water for purification; likewise after crossing [a river] on dry land.
Upon conversing with a woman, a Śūdra, or a hermaphrodite (uṃbaṣṭha), or upon seeing a corpse or blood, if one desires to worship a deity, one should sip water and then sip water again.
If food adheres to the teeth like a tooth, even if it has entered the mouth, one should rinse after sipping water; if it remains stuck there, one should rinse at that time.
For the sake of the twilight prayers, for eating, or likewise for the sake of the ancestors,

one should not perform the *ācamana* ritual using the hand of a Śūdra during recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), or other purificatory rites. Having touched someone who has not been initiated according to one's own caste, one should perform the *āgneya* bath.
For the purpose of removing the smell and smear of soot and oil, one should use cow dung with warm water.
Gold and silver shall be purified by rubbing with a touchstone and heating;
copper is purified by acid, and a vessel of bell-metal by ashes.
All objects made of metal become pure by being washed with sour substances or ashes;
bamboo, wood, and the like are purified by scrubbing with leaves such as those of the *kubja* tree,
while a clay alms-bowl becomes pure by being soaked in water overnight.
Those who have touched wood with impure hands become pure by purifying it with water.
One should wash pearls with conch shells or mother-of-pearl, but not with wheat;
however, one should then rub rice with the husks of wheat or the husks of rice.
It is proclaimed that for garments made of cloth, leather, bark, or hemp, purification is achieved with alkaline water. The same applies to blankets made of wool.
By constantly scrubbing all food vessels used for eating,
and likewise by heating water vessels over fire on all sides;
For those born from the bark [of trees], with water mixed with honey;
for all aquatic plants and likewise for bamboo products, with water;
and for eating from vessels such as bowls, leaves, and gourds. (7)
In this context, the purification of those things that have been used is prescribed by their abandonment.
Those things produced from bamboo that have come into contact with feces, urine, or desired objects must be discarded;
however, anything produced from all types of metals becomes pure once touched by fire.
A bowl licked by insects, mice, or cats is purified by seven strokes with a blade, by washing with water,
and also by circling it with fire.
One should discard what has been smelled or licked by a donkey, a camel, or similar animals;
indeed, a vessel that has been smelled by a cow must also be completely abandoned.
Likewise, a vessel or even clarified butter that has been licked by mongooses [must be discarded].
Indeed, it attained purification by being discharged from Agni seventy times.
Like a vessel, it attains purity through water and the like;
it is abundant, consumed by fire, frequented by crows and other such creatures, and devoid of measure.
If one touches food that has been left over by another, or food placed near the sacred fires,
one should rinse the mouth (ācamana) and then touch the food with water containing [the seeds of] darbha grass.

The purification of oily objects is by means of drying agents; the purification of smeared objects is by removing the smear; and the purification of foul-smelling things is by removing the odor with fragrant substances. (6) A seat, a bed, and a vehicle attain purification through earth and water.
The hand of a servant, the hand of an artisan, and the hand of one engaged in the sale of merchandise—with these one should deal with respect.
Fruit that is not spoiled, washed with water, or pecked at by birds;
[substances] purified by ash, by digging, or by being burnt; and those smeared on a clean rock;
[food] found on a street or path, which is pure due to the wind and the rays of the moon and sun. (7)
That which is defiled by flies or hair, or that which has been stepped upon by a foot; food containing dust or ants, or that which has been looked at while one is eating—
one should remove only that much and sprinkle it with water.

Purification occurs either by sprinkling clarified butter or by the scattering of ashes. However, cooked food exceeding one *droṇa* that has been defiled by crows, dogs, or other such creatures [requires further rites].
Having extracted a morsel [of the substance], an equal amount of ghee should be added;
one should then sprinkle it with water containing gold or, alternatively, with silver water.
(3) One should avoid [substances] that have been tasted by crows, dogs, and the like, or those that weigh less than one *droṇa*.
That food shall become purified by the Vedic chanting of the Brahmins.
(4) This applies at weddings with abundant food, when sacrifices are being performed,
during times such as consecrations, and even on the days of initiation festivals.
Food touched by crows or dogs attains purity through digging,
filling, burning, as well as by scrubbing or smearing.
From the time of committing a grave sin, one is purified by seven circumambulations.
(6) Even a dog-cooker (*śvapaca*) and one who reviles Śiva, if they are addicted to extremist views, should be released [from that state] by means of earth and water. (7)
One should discard earthen vessels and smear [the ground] with cow dung;
then, by means of gold, kuśa grass, and water, accompanied by the Brāhmaṇas and those initiated for the rite.
One should sprinkle all the vessels with water; then one will become pure, of this there is no doubt.
If cohabitation should occur, one should prescribe burning and heating.
Water that has been used for one night must be discarded, as must water that is impure or defiled by itself;
likewise, there is no purification required even when wells or ponds have been contaminated.
(2) This applies also when water has been left overnight or when it is mixed with bones, hides, dogs, donkeys, or the like.
Having removed one hundredth part of the jars, one should then pour in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Furthermore, when reservoirs of water are small,
one should avoid that bathing place (*tīrtha*) on this vast earth if it has been touched by the impure hands of *caṇḍālas* and others.
That which is frequented by fools and inhabited by women,
and which is touched by mosquitoes and flies, is not defiled.
And that which has been worn by a woman, a triple-layered garment, or one made of jewels;
likewise, the dwelling of a Brahmin, a threshing floor, and a temple;
(5) as well as that which is always pure, and the cow-pen of cows—these are pure.
Everywhere the earth is pure where no smearings are found. Even those made of tree leaves— which are themselves of an impure nature— their leaves, flowers, and fruits are not at all defiled.
Actors, dancers, carpenters, leather-workers, and goldsmiths; (7) those who rub posts, eunuchs, and prostitutes—these are proclaimed as those whose food should not be eaten.
A wife, a wine-maker, a female tailor,
a weaver, a wheelwright, a cobbler, a dyer, a seller of dog-meat, and likewise a thief.
One who lives by the profession of a banner-bearer, a Śūdra, a physician, a beggar, a potter, a painter, a usurer, and a seller of leather; (I.34a)
One should not accept a gift from a pregnant woman without first ascertaining her status; one should inquire [of the donor] whether she is pregnant, for she may be a woman who causes a miscarriage.
One who marries a woman of the same *gotra*, one who sells merit,
one who causes confusion among the *niṣādas*, and one who is devoid of the initiation of Śiva;
(3) one who subsists on the stage [and] one who is a secret agent...
A physician, a Cāgara, a Rūpajīvin, and a beggar.

A butcher, a seller of meat, one who has undertaken a vow at the beginning of a sacrifice, and whoever else among Brāhmaṇas engages in these activities out of delusion— (4)— [they are all to be avoided].
Even if he has performed the penance, he remains excluded;
for by these [acts], all Brāhmaṇas become Cāṇḍālas.

Therefore, those who perceive the truth avoid both the gods and the ancestors. [They avoid] wandering mendicants, those seeking worldly gain, and those whose life-force has departed while remaining in the state of asceticism;
likewise, those with matted hair, those with shaven heads, those bearing sectarian marks, and those consecrated by Śiva who have lost their life-force.
Whoever, having fashioned a *liṅga* or an image and the like in a place where [these] were excavated,
should worship it, by him the self-born [Lord] and others have been worshipped ten thousand times for every one thousand terrible [transgressions] committed, or even once.
Then, having performed the peace rite (*śānti*) resulting from the recitation for those desiring their own welfare,
[one should worship] Vīrabhadra, the Teacher, Durgā, Kālī, and Reṇukā.
One who honors Sthāneśa, Bhūteśa, the Gaṇas, and Virās, as well as those devoted to them and their own primary deities, is indeed praiseworthy; he who does not do so is censured.
One should not, even in one's mind, perform the viewing or salutation of a *liṅga* or an image (*bera*) worshipped by a *śūdra*, even if it is beautifully decorated with devotion.
(3) [Nor should one do so] with regard to that which has been worshipped by a *śūdra* there, whether out of delusion or even through ignorance.
He would become equal to a Śūdra, and his very life would be censured.
Or if one views or pays homage to the stable image of Īśvara with others, such as the Kāpālikas and so forth, that gives rise to a great fault. (4)
One who is one-eyed, one whose wife is barren, a physician, a singer,
one who performs worship for his own sake without [proper] intent, and likewise one who has sexual union with a Śūdra woman.

One who has not received initiation, even if he is a knower of the four Vedas, shall neither touch nor worship [the deity]. A Brahmin initiated into Śaivism shall not [perform rites] according to the Vaikhānasa Sūtra, nor those related to the Pāñcarātra, out of a desire for wealth for the sake of others. (6)
One should perform the worship of Śiva and Keśava for three years.
One who foolishly bears the conch, the discus, and the linga upon his body is called a *savaidevalaka*, and is censured in all ritual acts. (7)
One should know that a heretic is excluded from all ritual acts;
if he should touch [the vessel], it must be sprinkled with a thousand *ghora* mantras once it has been worshipped. (I.35a)
One with deformed nails, one with black teeth, or even one afflicted by a major disease;
a celibate student who is without a wife, or one who consumes liquor and meat;
one endowed with missing or extra limbs, or likewise one suffering from leprosy, white leucoderma, or being childless.
Whether he be tainted by a great sin (mahāpātaka), or one who has fallen from his vows (vidhūra), or likewise a wandering ascetic (yati);
If one should immediately perform worship for the sake of another, the king's kingdom will perish.
To avoid that fault, one should perform a propitiatory rite and a sprinkling with water.
He who fails to observe the fast on the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, or on the day of the Ārdrā asterism, or during the month of Carma, shall indeed become an object of reproach.
Furthermore, one who is engaged in [forbidden] ascetic practices becomes afflicted with vitiligo and leprosy.
And at the time of worshipping Hara, one should not even mentally allow for the sight or speech of those who are naked or otherwise contrary to the rules; however,
if it is for the sake of others, he may be worshipped according to the practice of the Raudrāgama.
One who knows the established doctrine need not perform [the rite];
however, if it must be performed, one should discard earthen vessels and proceed with the sprinkling of water.
If one shares a seat, a bed, a bath, or engages in the ritual of Śiva-pūjā with those who have been so declared, an expiation must certainly be performed.
If one performs the worship of Śiva at night when [the daily rites] have been performed only once,
one should always perform the worship of the *iṣṭaliṅga*, the fire-oblation (*homa*), the ritual bath, and the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*).
This applies except during a lunar eclipse and except for optional rites (*kāmya*) such as those performed at the twilights.
Purity, sipping water for purification, bathing, wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads;
(2) sprinkling, the aghamarṣaṇa rite, the twilight devotions, meditation, libations,
the ritual placement of mantras on the hands and limbs, the chanting of mantras, and circumambulation.
The daily rite of salutation to the deities of the directions is prescribed as a constant duty;
whether performed knowingly or unknowingly, upon the omission of even a single one, [there is a fault].
One should recite the Ghoramantra once for the purification of each respective sin;
if one desires worldly objects and, through negligence, worships Śiva at night, [one should likewise recite it].
If a king has eaten food obtained through fear of thieves, he becomes pure by bathing once it is digested;
if it is not digested, he should induce vomiting, bathe, and recite the Ghorasahasraka mantra.
Having bathed again according to the rules, he should worship his chosen *liṅga*.
And one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times at each [session].
O Śambhu, one who desires liberation should by all means perform worship and meditation;
if one fails to worship even once, one should recite the Ghorasahasra mantra a thousand times.
If done unintentionally, it is as previously stated; if intentional, it is double.
For him, there may be worship once a day, twice a day, or three times a day.
The third expiation for him is prescribed for both cases:
beginning from the second day, one should perform a thousand [recitations] with the Aghora mantra.
One should pass the day with a recitation of thirty thousand. In the case of the omission of the fortnightly worship, one should mutter twenty million of the *ghora* mantra;
in the case of the omission of the monthly worship, one should mutter ten million of the *bahurūpin* mantra.
The purification for a month or a year is performed by an increase of three myriads [of repetitions];
beyond that, purification is achieved through initiation (dīkṣā), as the worship of Śiva has been interrupted.

When one's own chosen liṅga has been stolen by thieves, mice, or humans; or when it is burnt, broken, cut, lost, or carried away by a stream; ||| (3) ||| The result is that one becomes a pauper, a servant, or a slave, or is born as a woman, a eunuch, or a low-caste person. ||| (4) ||| Therefore, one should always protect one's own liṅga with great effort, just as one would protect one's own life. ||| (5) ||| If the liṅga is lost, one should install another liṅga made of clay or stone, or even one fashioned from wood. ||| (6) ||| One should worship that very same deity who was worshipped in the previous liṅga, and never worship another deity. ||| (7) ||| If the liṅga is lost, one should perform the rite of installation (pratiṣṭhā) again according to the prescribed rule, or else one should perform the rite of re-installation (punar-pratiṣṭhā). ||| (8) ||| Alternatively, having bathed the liṅga with water and sprinkled it with sandalwood paste, one should worship it with flowers and other offerings. ||| (9) ||| Or, having placed the liṅga within a vessel filled with water, one should worship it there until another liṅga can be obtained. ||| (10) ||| If the liṅga is lost due to the fault of the officiating priest (purohita), the king, or the subjects, the king shall incur sin and go to hell. ||| (11) ||| Therefore, the king, the priest, and the subjects must all protect the liṅga with every effort, as they would their own life. ||| (12) ||| Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Protection of the Liṅga," in the Śivarahasya, the fifth part of the Skanda Purāṇa. ||| (13) ||| Chapter 44: The Description of the Installation of the Liṅga. ||| (1) ||| Śiva said: ||| O Goddess, I shall now describe the procedure for the installation of the liṅga, which bestows all desired fruits. ||| (2) ||| Having first performed the preliminary rites such as the selection of the site (bhūmi-parigraha) and the purification of the ground (bhūmi-śuddhi), one should then perform the ritual of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila-karma). ||| (3) ||| One should draw a lotus diagram (padma-maṇḍala) on the sacrificial ground using five-colored powders, and place a conch shell and a golden vessel upon it. ||| (4) ||| Then, having consecrated the liṅga with mantras and placed it within a vessel, one should worship it with perfumes, incense, lamps, and food offerings. ||| (5) ||| One should then perform the rite of invocation (āvāhana) and the rite of seating (āsana), and worship the Lord with the primary mantra (mūla-mantra) and the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra). ||| (6) ||| One should offer oblations (homa) into the fire with clarified butter and sesame seeds, reciting the mantra "Om Hram Śivāya Namah" one hundred and eight times. ||| (7) ||| Then, having circumambulated the liṅga three times and bowed down, one should perform the rite of re-consecration (punar-pratiṣṭhā) with the mantra "Om Hrim Śivāya Namah. ||| (8) ||| One should then perform the rite of the final offering (arghya) and the rite of dismissal (udvāsana), and worship the Lord with flowers, incense, and other offerings. ||| (9) ||| Thus, O Goddess, I have described the procedure for the installation of the liṅga; by performing this, one attains all desires. ||| (10) ||| Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Installation of the Liṅga," in the Śivarahasya, the fifth part of the Skanda Purāṇa. ||| (11) ||| Chapter 45: The Description of the Greatness of the Liṅga. ||| (1) ||| Śiva said: ||| O Goddess, listen now to the greatness of the liṅga, which destroys all sins and grants liberation. ||| (2) ||| By worshipping the liṅga, one attains heaven; by worshipping it constantly, one attains liberation. ||| (3) ||| Even those who are sinful, those who are ignorant, and those who are devoid of merit—by worshipping the liṅga, they all attain the highest state. ||| (4) ||| Whether it be a stone, a piece of wood, or even a lump of clay—if it is installed as a liṅga, it becomes the giver of all fruits. ||| (5) ||| There is no other deity superior to the liṅga; the liṅga is the supreme Brahman, the liṅga is the supreme goal. ||| (6) ||| The liṅga is the soul of all beings, the liṅga is the source of the universe. By meditating upon the liṅga, one attains union with Śiva. ||| (7) ||| Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Liṅga," in the Śivarahasya, the fifth part of the Skanda Purāṇa. ||| (8) ||| Chapter 46: The Description of the Ritual of Bathing the Liṅga. ||| (1) ||| Śiva said: ||| O Goddess, I shall now describe the ritual of bathing the liṅga, which bestows all auspiciousness and destroys all diseases. ||| (2) ||| Having prepared a vessel filled with pure water and mixed with sandalwood paste, saffron, and camphor, one should bathe the liṅga with that water. ||| (3) ||| One should bathe the liṅga with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta)—milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar—and then bathe it with fragrant water. ||| (4) ||| Then, having dressed the liṅga in fine garments and adorned it with ornaments, one should worship it with flowers, incense, and lamps. ||| (5) ||| One should offer food offerings (naivedya) consisting of various sweets and fruits, and recite hymns of praise to the Lord of the Universe. ||| (6) ||| By bathing the liṅga in this manner, one attains long life, health, wealth, and progeny; and at the end, one attains liberation. ||| (7) ||| Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual of Bathing the Liṅga," in the Śivarahasya, the fifth part of the Skanda Purāṇa. ||| (8) ||| Chapter 47: The Description of the Greatness of the Five Liṅgas. ||| (1) ||| Śiva said: ||| O Goddess, listen to the greatness of the five liṅgas, which bestows all desired fruits and destroys all sins. ||| (2) ||| The first is the Sthāṇuliṅga, the second is the Tryambakaliṅga, the third is the Raudraliṅga, the fourth is the Vṛṣabhaliṅga, and the fifth is the Śrīkaṇṭhaliṅga. ||| (3) ||| By worshipping these five liṅgas, one attains the fivefold fruits: knowledge, power, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. ||| (4) ||| Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Five Liṅgas," in the Śivarahasya, the fifth part of the Skanda Purāṇa. ||| (5) ||| Chapter 48: The Description of the Ritual of Offering Flowers to the Liṅga. ||| (1) ||| Śiva said: ||| O Goddess, I shall now describe the ritual of offering flowers
One should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times and install another linga;
this is declared to be its purification, and the same applies to the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
Indeed, for movable and immovable images as well as their pedestals, the procedure is exactly that.
From a slight blow by a staff or similar object, [the mantra] is purified by ten thousand recitations;
from a major blow, it is purified by double that amount for the Aghora mantra.
When one's chosen *liṅga* has been rolled over, one should recite the Ghora mantra one thousand times.

If the *liṅga* falls twice, the recitation should be doubled; if it rolls three or four times, one hundred thousand recitations should be added; and if it falls from the pit, one should perform the recitation with the *bahurūpī* mantra.

If the *liṅga* falls upon the base (*ādhāra*), one should recite the mantra together with the *tāla* and *tāla*; however, if it falls without the base, one should recite it twice as much. In cases of intentional or unintentional [falling], it is as previously stated.
If the *liṅga* falls due to pride in manliness or out of desire from a state of total attachment,
and it becomes worn out or decayed, no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed for that.
If one breaks a linga or a śalākā, his sin shall be great;
for purification, he should perform three hundred thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra. (2) Regarding sexual intercourse with a liṅga, there is no prescribed atonement whatsoever.
If the linga is touched by the foot or even stepped over, one must recite twenty thousand [times].
If the water from the hand touches the *liṅga* of Ghoras, ten thousand [repetitions] must be performed;
the wise should perform a ritual bath for the *liṅga* in all such cases where it has been defiled.
If the linga has been touched by phlegm or water mixed with phlegm,
it is declared that one should perform thirty thousand or twenty thousand recitations with the Bahurūpa mantra.
When the *liṅga* is sprinkled with water consecrated by [the mantras of] the Mothers, it is joined with twenty thousand (*ayuta*) [repetitions];
when adorned with the forms of blood, semen, and menstrual flow, it is joined with fifty thousand (*pañcaka*).
When the *liṅga* is touched with water consecrated by those [mantras], it is joined with [the same number] less one-quarter.
If the *liṅga* is touched by feces, one should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times;

likewise for being struck by a foot, or for contact with water used for bathing [the deity], or with the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*). If the *liṅga* falls while smeared with feces, one must recite fifty thousand [mantras].
If the Liṅga has been touched by persons who have not received initiation, the expiation prescribed there is one, two, or three hundred repetitions of the Aghora-Śambara mantra. (7)
If the *liṅga* is touched by a Śūdra, one should mutter [the mantra] five hundred times;
if it is touched by fishermen, actors, and the like, ten thousand times;
and if the *liṅga* is touched by crows and other such creatures, one should mutter it twenty thousand times.
When the Liṅga has been beheld by outcastes, one should recite [the mantra] fifty thousand times.
If one touches that [liṅga], one should mutter the Ghoraśambara mantra twice as many times;
if one touches a liṅga situated on either the left or right path, one should mutter it an equal number of times.
If the liṅga is moved from its pedestal and remains free of defects,
one should re-install it in that very place and mutter the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times.
(3) One should discard that liṅga if it is defective or has been used by outcastes and the like.
Having installed another linga, one attains purification.
In the case of the Nirvāṇa fire or the fire belonging to the Lord (Īśvara), one should observe a fast for three nights in the event of the omission of ritual action,
the violation of a rule, or the failure to make offerings.
One should recite the Śaiva Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times over them;
when the eight bonds are severed, there shall be worship of the Liṅga for the ascetic.
If even a mere drop falls upon the portion of Bharata, or even upon the portion of Brahmā,
or when it reaches the portion of Rudra, a great fault arises.

If at that time the worship is performed only once, twice, or thrice [per day], it is said to be fruitless; there will be misfortune for the king and distress for the kingdom. To perform it, or even to cause it to be performed, in such a manner would bring about great calamity.
It should be performed as if it were for that very moment, without specifying the month, fortnight, or day.
Having performed the sprinkling with water, thereafter one should perform the pacificatory oblation;
having recited the Aghora mantra more than a hundred thousand times, one should carry out the reintegration.
On the day of the sun’s transit, on the fourteenth, the eighth, and also on the two festival days (parvan),
if the lamp is extinguished in the temple of Hari, the fault is fourfold due to the constant neglect.
Furthermore, during the months beginning with Āṣāḍha, when the sacred thread ceremony (pavitrāropaṇa) is performed, [the same applies].
One should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred thousand times and then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having performed the rite of purification while avoiding the conduct prescribed therein,
even if one has gone to another village during the interval between the four-month periods;
If the *pavitra* rite is omitted, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance for purification;
likewise, if the offering of *damanaka* flowers and other rites are not performed, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
While the vessel for the *arghya* offering and other vessels have not yet been dismissed,
one should recite two hundred *ghora* mantras during the withdrawal (*vivarta*) and the entry (*viśna*).
In due order, these five hundred [recitations] amount to a thousand there.
The purification of the rosary and the linga shall be performed from the upper half of the foot.
If the thread is broken while it is newly spun, one should recite the *ghora* mantra one thousand times;
if the old thread is not yet severed, one should recite the *ghora* mantra one hundred times.
Having placed the beautiful rosary from his hand upon the ground,
and having washed it with water and worshipped it, he should recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times. Then,
by ringing the bell, he should offer [the oblation] starting from the eighth part above the liṅga.
One should prepare the ritual implements for worship and so forth as previously described.
The master of mantras should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred times while touching with his foot;
for one desiring worldly results, ten thousand recitations are required there, while for children and others, it is a quarter [of that].
If the food offering is defiled by hair, insects, bones, meat, or other such things, one should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred times; if there is a desire for results, then ten thousand times.
If inferior offerings are presented, there is a constant fear of two terrible [rebirths];

if one offers incense made from the limbs of living beings, it is considered that one must undergo a hundred births as a *sadyojāta* (newborn). (3) If one treads upon a *liṅga*, or touches one's gurus, the fire of Śiva, or...
Purification from an intentional act [of eating] at the Aghora [fire] requires sixty thousand [repetitions]; from that [same act] unintentionally, it is sixfold [that many].
For violating the command of the teachers Śivacaṇḍas, one hundred thousand [is the fine];
for the characteristics of one who is inferior among them, one hundred thousand less a quarter is prescribed.
In the characteristics of the *nirmālya*... the purification of the feet is mastery;
giving is equal to eating, and half of that [benefit] is obtained by looking at it. (5)

If one consumes [the remains of an offering] unintentionally, or if it is the *nirmālya* (remains of a deity's garland), one should, being purified, recite the *Brahma-pañcaka* one thousand times, or half of that according to the *Saṃhitā*.
(6) In the case of intentional consumption, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the expiation; there is no other.
If one steps over the remains of offerings (nirmālya), one should then mutter the mantra ten thousand times with great care.
Touching it is equal to leaping over [the deity], and there is no transformation in eating it;
the first [type] of that deity's sixfold *nirmālya* is thus considered. (7)

Furthermore, the characteristics of divine property (*devadravya*), the offering (*naivedya*) presented thereafter, the substance for Caṇḍa (*caṇḍadravya*), and the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) are now described:
divine property consists of the land, fields, and so forth belonging to the deity, as well as gold and clothing.
The cooked offering of fragrance and other items, presented as the remains of Śiva's meal (śivocchiṣṭa), has been offered.
Caṇḍa is Caṇḍadatta; the *nirmālya* has been wiped away outside.
(2) Even when the Lord of Gaurī has been dismissed, the *nirmālya* does not remain on the pedestal.

By giving away the remains of an offering (*nirmālya*), one becomes a flesh-eating demon; by eating it, one becomes a lowliest of men, a *mātaṅga*; and by stepping over it, there is a fall from spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
By giving away its fragrance, one becomes a jackal; and by [stepping over] it, one becomes a *caṇḍāla*.
A Śabara woman may sell it, and [a man] would incur womanhood by touching it.
Whatever substance has been touched by the remains of offerings (nirmālya), even if it is consumed by the hands,
one should prescribe for that the previously mentioned penance reduced by one-quarter.
Whatever flowers and other offerings have entered the inner sanctum by way of incidental contact, they become *caṇḍāṃśa* [polluted] due to that contact with the *nirmālya*; of this there is no doubt.
Having consumed that, at the time of Śiva’s worship, the continuous flow of incense, perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
as well as the light of various lamps and such, does not cause any fault. (6)

Until the conclusion of the fourth rite, the wise person should not consume food, medicine, flowers, water, leaves, fruits, or any other offerings that have been presented to Śiva as *nirmālya*. Having offered these to Śiva, one should eat only what remains from those offerings. (7)
He who, though initiated by Śiva, consumes what has not been given, which is undesirable and unfit for consumption,
becomes purified by reciting the Root Mantra one hundred and eight times and performing worship;
there is no doubt that it is like the sacrificial oblation (caru) offered to his own chosen Liṅga.
Having eaten that, one shall obtain the complete fruit of the worship of Śiva;
likewise, [the fruit of] the consecration of deities, as well as of tanks and gardens.
One should recite [the mantra] five hundred times here, and not after eating food on the fifth lunar day.
At the Svayambhū, Daivika, and Bāṇa [shrines], there is no offering of used garlands (nirmālya).
Likewise, there is no used garland for any of the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Having eaten food at the *puṃsavana* rite, one should mutter the *vāmadeva* hymn a hundred times.
He who eats on the eleventh day, or even on the twelfth day and so forth,
should mutter either one hundred thousand or three hundred thousand recitations of the *ghora* mantra.
Every month, during the Śivarātri festival, one should recite the three hundred [verses] of the Ghoramantra.
One should likewise avoid the food of the Gaṇas, the food of courtesans, and the food of renunciants.
And having eaten the food of a beggar, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
likewise after a cooked sacrifice, a marriage, the gift of a cow, or the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass.
By eating the food of Brahmins who have fallen from their conduct, one does not incur the sin of consuming forbidden food;
for whatever caste eats the food of another without being formally invited, [that food is considered as if consumed by its own caste].
Having combined the lord of that class with the lord of its own class, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times.
One should perform the rites of eating once, twice, thrice, or four times, in sequence.
(I.39b) The lords of the castes, such as the Brahmins and others, are the masters of the [respective] classes of men.
O twice-born ones devoted to Śiva, it has been thus declared that Īśāna belongs only to other castes.
In the event of indigestion, a wise person should abandon recitation, ritual bathing, worship, and fire-offerings;
however, once the food is digested, one should bathe and then recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having touched one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), or one who is impure due to food remnants (*samucchiṣṭa*), or a person of the same caste (*savarṇaka*),

a wise man should repeat the mantra of his own clan-lord (*svajātīśa*) one hundred and eight times. (3) Having touched one who has been initiated along with the gods (*sadeva-dīkṣita*), he should bathe and then recite it two hundred times.
A Brahmin, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra who have been consecrated for a sacrifice may eat even the leavings of food.
Having been initiated and having fasted for two nights or three nights,
one should merge the Lord of that [element] with the Lord of its own [corresponding element] and recite [the mantra] in sequence.
Having touched the leavings of food belonging to a king or a Śūdra, one should fast for two days;
then, having combined the lords of those respective classes with the lord of one's own class, one should recite [the mantra] in sequence.
Having touched those who have not been initiated, one should perform twice the penance previously mentioned.
Therefore, a king is purified by half [of that], and a Vaiśya is purified by a quarter less;
a Śūdra attains purification by a fourth part—of this there is no doubt. (6)
And when one has consumed the food-remnants of another, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times for the lord of one's own caste.
One who eats the food of the lowly or the leavings of another is the worst; he should perform twice that penance.
Having fasted and bathed with purity, he is fit for consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (7)
O Brahmacārins, this vow is prescribed for you everywhere;
likewise, one should abandon one's own preferred sectarian marks from the great heart and [discard] the lakes.
If that which was taken from thieves, kings,
or others is recovered after some time has passed, how should the twice-born man honor it?
(2) Having sprinkled it with water, he should perform the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*).
Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times, and the root mantra an equal number of times.
One should perform worship at both lingas constantly and without sloth;
having first worshipped that which is smeared with unguents, one should thereafter worship that which is smeared with ashes.
This expiation has been declared for householders according to the sequence;
a student (brahmacārī) should perform it twofold, and a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) threefold.
A renunciant (saṃnyāsī) should perform the expiation fourfold.
If the worship of the gatekeepers is omitted, there will be great affliction from obstacles.
Having completed half of that with the *saṃhitā-homa*, one should worship the gatekeepers;
for one who is devoid of the five purifications (*pañcaśuddhi*), that worship which has been performed becomes [fruitless].
It does not, however, arise from one who is ill-established;
rather, it arises from a man who is free from the ten defilements. (6)
Furthermore, when there is a deviation from the sequence— such as by using offerings like milk-rice, cakes, sugarcane juice, and so forth—
the [deities] are distressed, and confusion arises on earth.
But when there is a failure in the removal of the veil over the Vidyā and so forth, the teacher must observe the defects of those being examined;
having then performed a propitiatory fire-oblation (śānti-homa), he should perform everything as prescribed.
This applies to the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites when they are deficient in materials such as the water for the feet (pādya) and the like.
In this world, the destruction of those respective substances occurs through those respective limbs.
If the substance for the feet or that belonging to him is lacking, there will be foot disease;
likewise, if the water for rinsing the mouth is lacking, there will be a disease of the mouth.
If the bell is missing from its head, its base, or its parts, there will be loss;
if it is struck without being suspended from a chain, Piśācas, Rākṣasas, and other such beings will cause suffering and afflictions to those living in that region.
(3) Furthermore, calamities will arise and be known among the inhabitants of that place.
If the offering of lamps is deficient or omitted, there will be eye disease. If the invocation is omitted, or if the oblation (*havis*) or its constituent parts are omitted,
or if the food offering (*naivedya*) and its constituents are not presented, there will be the destruction of crops.
In that case, there will be the loss of wealth, and great hunger and thirst shall arise;
(5) in the absence of offering betel, or if the limb is deficient, there will be disease of the mouth.
Now, if on a low-quality blind-canvas painting there is a deficiency in the assembly of the deities,
one should worship the deity and cause that material to be given as double in value to Śiva.
Then one should perform a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) or lead the preceptors for the ritual bathing;
if the materials or limbs [of the rite] are deficient, O Śivā, one should cause double the amount to be given.
A *saṃhitā-homa* must be performed, or alternatively, the recitation of the *Aghora* mantra a hundred times.
Of these substances, [the proportions] are thus: half, a quarter, and half of that.
Having recited the principal *aghora* mantra two hundred and six times in sequence,
one should then cause that substance to be given to the deity as a double portion.
If these materials are offered to Śaṅkara without the mantra, the preceptor, having worshipped them for the gods, should give those materials back; at the end,
he should offer the material with his own mantra, either doubled or in equal measure.
One should cause the desired ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed, which involves the recitation of the Aghora mantra one hundred times.
In the obligatory, occasional, or optional rites, if there is an omission of the three items beginning with water for the feet,
one who does not accomplish the practice should recite the mantras of Sadyojāta, Nareśa, and Īśāna a hundred times.
One should offer double the usual amount of water for the feet and other offerings, or simply the substance itself.
If [the ritual] is deficient in dūrvā grass, flowers, and unbroken rice, it is prescribed that one should recite the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra) one hundred times.
This applies when the oil massage, the rubbing powder, the bath, and so forth have already begun.
If [the debtor] is of low status, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times with the heart and cause him to pay double again.
In the worship with unconditioned ingredients such as sesame oil and others, there is the *saṃhitā-huti* (the combined oblation).
In the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, [the oblation is] as previously determined, consisting of five or ten [units].
If the *saṃhitā-homa* has been omitted, one should perform it twice;
by this procedure, expiation is accomplished through the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
If the previously intended scent is lost, one should immediately recite the mantra a hundred times;
then one should offer that substance either doubled or in equal measure.
Or, if it is deficient or lacking, one should offer a flower, or conversely.
One should recite the mantra of Īśa one hundred times, and then twice that number with the respective substances.
Having recited the terrible *dhūpārātrika* mantra twice its length at the conclusion,
one should then perform the offering of incense (*dhūpa*), the night-rite (*rātrika*), and the waving of lights (*nīrājana*) at the appropriate time.
If [the wick] is severed, one should restore it by re-preparing it after it has been spun a hundred times.
When the Lord is obscured by a row of lamps or by the mouth of a mouse and the like, [one should act accordingly].
If the emblem (*liṅga*), the image (*bera*), the body (*aṅga*), or other such parts are touched by fire,
or if even a minute particle has entered [the deity], the king will fall ill. Having purified what was struck by fire according to the prescribed rite, one should bathe the Supreme Lord.
Combined with the five nectars (pañcamṛta) and accompanied by coconut water.
Having fully worshipped the Lord of the Gods of gods, one should perform the ritual oblation to the images;
(4) if the fire should become as small as an atom, one should perform a rite of pacification.
If the linga, the pedestal, and so forth, as well as the garments, have been consumed by fire,
one should perform a rite consisting of ritual sprinkling.
If [the image] is burnt in part, one should perform a pacification rite;
one should perform a sprinkling with pure water for the sake of the self’s burning and lead it away.
(6) One should perform a ceremonial bath for the deity when damage to its abode or similar occurrences arise.
Therefore it has been said: "One should perform the expiation (niṣkṛti), provided with the joining (sandhāna) and other [required rites]."

When the linga, image, or other [object] assumes another color due to fire, if it is of human origin, it should be abandoned; if it is of self-manifested (svāyambhuva) or other divine origin, it should be accepted.
One should perform the remedial rite as prescribed, accompanied by sprinkling;
having offered incense at the various limbs of the body, one should recite the fifth [mantra] one hundred times.
In the event of a deficiency of lamps, one should recite the Ghoramantra three hundred times;
thereafter, one should cause the God of gods to be provided with double the number of lamps.
Even upon the interruption of the protective lamp, one should likewise perform the recitation twice over.
And having performed the ceremonial bathing of the deity to whom the sacrificial oblation has been offered;
If one subsequently invites [others] after having already committed to a sacrifice, one should be made to pay double;
likewise, if the blindfold is deficient, one should recite the Kavaca mantra two hundred times.
Salutation to the illustrious Medhā Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Every year, every month, the festival is prepared with its full array of provisions;
having determined beforehand on which days it was held in the past, it proceeds for nine days and so forth, preceded by the beating of kettledrums and other ceremonies. (4–5)
If the fire is made three times that day's measure, or even twice that day's measure,
but otherwise than that, there will surely be great harm to the kingdom and the king. (6) Having first performed a propitiatory rite therein, one should carry out the festival as before.
But it may also occur within another month, or even during that very same month.
On the second day, or on that very day, having performed the image-oblation (mūrtihoma) and the offerings to the quarters (diśāhuti) in due order,
the festival should be conducted according to the prescribed rules.
Prior to the hoisting of the banner, one should arrange three times the [required] number of days;
thus the procedure has been declared, and it should be inferred that the same applies to twice the [number of days].
If the *liṅga* is of self-manifested origin (*svāyambhuva*), this procedure is prescribed;
likewise for human-made *bāṇaliṅgas* and others, whether divine (*daiva*), celestial (*ārṣaka*), or otherwise.
The twice-born may perform the rites according to the month, the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), or otherwise as appropriate.
The festivals held on those previous days bestow the fruit of his prosperity.
In times of national upheaval, famine, or threats from kings and thieves,
as well as due to the lack of wealth and other such fears, it is— as previously stated— impossible to perform [the rites].
If [the birth] occurs there as well, one should first perform a rite of pacification;
or one may observe a day-fast and hold a festival according to the traditional path.
When all [the rites] are omitted, his merit is diminished and his festivals are lost;
when a total omission is made, a great fault arises for him.
(5) He should then perform the rite of pacification, the fire-oblation for peace, and the fire-oblation for the deity’s form.
By this procedure,
if a festival has been commenced by astrologers and others that is devoid of the rites for averting obstacles and the like, it will lead to the destruction of the kingdom;
therefore, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*) and then conduct the festival again.
If the consecration of the bull has been omitted even though the hoisting of the banner has taken place,
one should perform the śānti-homa as prescribed for the loss of cattle.
One should perform the bull-sacrifice there at the base of the flagstaff;
however, if the flag is destroyed, one should mentally perform the ritual placement of mantras and so forth.
If the raising of the flag is omitted, it portends danger for the king.
Having performed a rite of pacification, one should then consecrate the banner once more.
If the circumambulation of the banner is deficient, it brings misfortune to the village and its inhabitants;
therefore, one should perform a pacificatory fire-offering for the removal of all defects.
Whether the altar is devoid of characteristics or possesses them, it bestows auspiciousness;
having then performed a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should construct an altar endowed with the proper characteristics.
If the staff lacks its defining characteristics, it brings misfortune to the leader;
therefore, one should perform the *mūrtihoma* or likewise the *śāntihoma*.
If the staff is devoid of its own specific marks, it bestows both [misfortune] upon the subordinate and the leader.

Then one should perform a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*) for the destruction of pride regarding the *skandhas*. (6) When there occurs the breaking or splitting of the staff, the secondary staff, the *skandha*, and so forth, one should then perform a propitiatory oblation; if it is broken, one should proceed with another propitiation.
If the banner-flame is deficient, it brings fear to this kingdom;
therefore, one should undertake the planting of another banner-flame endowed with the proper characteristics.
In the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*), when the characteristics of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) are deficient during the raising of the banner,
one should likewise perform an expiation (*niṣkṛti*) with a bull to remove the fault.

If one does not follow the *ūrdhvacitra* manual, one should mutter the mantra of Īśa as a protection; or else, if one is devoid of that, no fault whatsoever arises. (3) Upon the cutting of the rope or by enemies' binding, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*).
If the cloth and other items are scorched by fire, one should then perform a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*).
(4) If the banner falls to the ground, it indicates misfortune for the kingdom;
having then performed the propitiatory oblation according to the rules, one should raise the flag once more. (5)
When there is damage to the banner or similar incidents, one should then perform a rite of pacification;
within seven days, O twice-born, one should raise another flag.
O twice-born ones, if each preceding [type of] sacrifice results in little merit,
then one should perform either the *mūrtihoma* or the *śāntihoma*.
If this banner is blown away by the wind or the like,
or if it is damaged by the onset of defects, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma) for its pacification.
If the garland of darbha grass is missing, then one should likewise perform the propitiatory fire-sacrifice.

Then, one should wrap a staff possessing the proper characteristics with a garland of *darbha* grass. Alternatively, having joined either a rope or a garland of *darbha* grass to the staff in a clockwise manner, one should recite the Aghora mantra a thousand times.
One should lead the darbha garland and other items forward in a clockwise sequence from the front;
likewise, one should perform the *upadaṇḍa* rite with the *kūrca* and mutter the *ghora* mantra three hundred times.
If the bell on the banner is missing and the bull [emblem] should not be present,
the preceptor should likewise recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times.
If the bell falls to the ground, he should mutter the Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra three hundred times.
A binding that is too tight is not desired for the purpose of punishment, O Śivā. However,
at the time of hoisting the banner, if the ritual placement of the water-pot (kumbha-nyāsa) has not been performed,
one should cause the bull, the pot, and the elephant to ascend the pole.
Having performed the *śānti*-oblation and established the water-pots as before,
one should then perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) mentally within the heart-lotus.
If one performs the consecration with the water from the jars that remove those obstructions,
one should perform a recitation of one hundred repetitions for each individual mantra.
When that banner has been raised and lowered by means of the *laya* [rhythm],
it is fashioned according to the measure of one, two, three, or four [units]. (2) Then,
one should recite the *Aghora* mantra three hundred times, ending with the downward-measured *vimātrā*.
And having performed the propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) while the banner (ketu) is hanging down from that [pole], |||
Thereafter, one should raise the banner accompanied by the worship of the bull;
for if the beating of the drum is omitted, delusion arises in the world.
Having then performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should thereafter strike the drum;
for the recitation of the Bṛhatsāman, one should perform the peace-rite.
If the invocation of the deities is not performed prior to the commencement of the festival,
there will be no presence of the gods and other beings.
One should first perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) and then carry out the invocation of the deities according to the Vedic rites.

When Keśāmbā, Skanda, Vidhneśa, Bhānu, Caṇḍeśvara, and Īśvara [are worshipped], there is no fault if they have not been formally invited; however, in times of calamity, one should not fail to invite them. One should not install the nine [deities] without first performing the raising of the banner.
In the case of striking a drum, one should act in exactly the same manner;
that is, when there is the occurrence of cutting the skin and so forth, or cutting the nose and so forth.
Having recited the Aghora-weapon mantra a hundred times, one should then strike another drum.
In the same manner, having taken up another bell, one should proceed as before.
(2) Or, if the bell falls to the ground, one should recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times.
At that time, or at the time of the *bali* offering, if the drum falls to the ground,
one should then perform a *śānti-homa* to prevent the misfortune of the kingdom.
If the kettle-drum falls to the ground, there will be great danger for the king.
Then, having performed the propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa), one should worship the drum with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra).
Whether the sacrificial hall has been consumed by fire or is devoid of its characteristic features, [one should proceed].
Whether it be a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), a sacrificial altar (*kuṇḍavedī*), a kingdom, or a state of distress,
one should first have them properly constructed during every festival;
daily rites for peace (*śāntihoma*) should be performed until the day of the consecration.
Having understood that festival and the characteristics of the sacrificial hall, he [acted].
I shall then perform the rite of pacification so that no fault remains;
this general procedure applies both to the consecration and to the expiation.
During the sprinkling with water, the ritual aspersion, the worship and so forth, or the removal of the thread;
or during the festive rites, or otherwise, in the procedure for the restoration of a dilapidated temple using bricks.
One should employ [the mantra] in obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, as well as in other activities;
likewise in the preparation for a sacrifice, but not at its conclusion.
The pacifying oblation (*śāntihoma*) should be performed for one day in both cases:
at the commencement of the primary rite and when there is a failure of the ritual implements.
(3) For the pacifying oblation, one should recite the Aghora-weapon mantra two hundred or three hundred times.
If [the vessels] are missing, one should not perform the *śānti*-oblation on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
To remove that defect, one should prepare the sacrificial mound as before.
This applies to the *śiva-kumbha*, the *vardhanī*, and the eight jars used for the circumambulation.
And in other vessels used for the limbs of the festival, as they may be,
there should be a sequence of distinct characteristics according to their specific differences, such as being solid, porous, or perforated.
One should perform four hundred recitations of the Śānti-homa and the Aghorāstra-mantra;
for the removal of diseases, one may likewise perform three hundred or one hundred recitations.
Having brought the nine vessels beginning with the *kumbha*, one should perform their installation as before.
The *vardhanī* or the *kalaśa* are presided over by the lords of the *dhṛtavidyā*.
They may be devoid of golden lotuses, or else provided with a small amount of gold.
By reciting the Aghora mantra one thousand times, one may cause poverty for the perpetrator;
however, to remove that fault, one should again bestow what is established by the scriptures.
If the ritual vessels, such as the water-pot and others, are deficient, wind-related diseases will afflict men.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times, the Guru should again present a garment;
even in the absence of the five gems and so forth, he should perform it in this very same manner.

Even in the absence of the prescribed ritual for the thread and the tuft of grass (*sūtrakūrca*), one should act in this manner. However, if the binding of the *kautuka* (protective thread) is deficient, that very limb [of the rite] is said to be fruitless when performed on the day prior; therefore, for the pacification of that defect, [one should perform the following].
Then one should perform the peace-offering (śānti-homa), and thereafter bind the protective amulet (kautuka).
One should mutter the Aghora mantra three hundred times for the removal of defects in its constituent parts;
likewise, having performed the immediate consecration (adhivāsana) upon that fire-rite, [one should proceed].
When the deity is established in his former place, the tying of the auspicious thread (kautuka-bandhana) is prescribed;
or, having brought [the deity] to the pavilion or similar location, one should recite the Ghoramantra fifty times.
One should recite the *japa* for the great *vedas* and the *tālas* such as *balitāla* while facing south;
likewise, the dancer (*naṭī*), having offered a handful of flowers, should also perform the recitation for the carriers of the sandals (*pādukāvāhaka*).
In the event of a fall, or if the performance is deficient, or likewise if the sandals fall,
there shall be three hundred recitations of the *ghora-mantra* and one thousand for the sandals.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*), one should then proceed with the circumambulation of the sandals.

In the event of the loss of three hundred lamps, one should perform twice as many lamp-offerings. (3) If a vehicle is missing during a festival, it brings all manner of faults upon men; one should therefore perform a ceremonial bath, a rite of pacification, a golden offering, and the re-consecration of the vehicle.

During times of rain, in a great wind, during a national upheaval, or in the face of great danger, it is not desired to circumambulate the village; rather, one should circumambulate the desired sanctuary.
O best of the twice-born, at that time the ceremonial bathing and the propitiatory fire-offering should be performed,
O lords of brahmins, while the festival of Śiva is taking place within a single sacred precinct.
If a different festival is celebrated there, it causes confusion for the village;
to eliminate that fault, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
Likewise, if the parents are not present, one should perform an expiation (prāyaścitta).
O Śaiva, those born from limb after limb, the Yāmalas, and the Autas are free from defects.
If the Vāmabhairava-siddha receives the bali offering, there will be the destruction of the village.
If it is offered through negligence regarding the bali, one should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
If a great offering is prepared while relying on an empty village, one should know that the destruction of the kingdom is at hand; if it has been performed, one should practice pacification.
Or, if the great offering is made in a dwelling, there will be an unfavorable turn of fortune for him.
It is especially recommended for a site belonging to the gods or for a site belonging to others.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, there were those dwelling nearby and those dwelling far away;
it was filled with various kinds of trees and endowed with many different species of trees.
The opposite of this is considered auspicious; otherwise, it brings about calamity.
Among the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, that which is superior is called the best.
Whether it be internal or external, it is distinguished by its strength and its expansion.
Or, when one is stronger than the other, it is called "superior."

This is indeed a secondary rule for those who are incapable; in such a case, one should perform it elsewhere. For those engaged in a secondary rite, one should perform a propitiatory oblation (śānti-homa).
If the canopy is deficient, one should proceed by reciting the Aghora-aṇu a hundred times;
likewise, even if the banner is missing, it shall be so after reciting the Aghora-aṇu a hundred times.
O best of the twice-born, there is no fault if the banner is missing at night;
however, if the offering materials are missing, men will suffer from the affliction of hunger.
Then, having performed the *mūrtihoma*, one should offer the *bali* at the end of the procession (*yāna*) or at the conclusion of the ritual.
When the temple is devoid of *bali* offerings, one should recite the *Aghora-mantra* one hundred times.
In whichever direction the village or other location lacks the *bali*, there the *saṃhitā-huti* [should be offered].
One should perform the recitation of the mantra one hundred times for each respective quarter.
One should carry the *bali* offering either at the time of departing or at its conclusion;
however, if it is devoid of the characteristic signs of food, famine arises on earth.
Therefore, having performed a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*), one should carry the *bali* together with the characteristic signs of food.
In cases of cutting, piercing, or [injuries to] the feet and so forth, one should likewise prescribe offerings of food (bali) and other such rites.
Having made that liṅga very firm, one should worship the weapon-mantra residing therein;
having performed the combined oblation (saṃhitā-homa) in that place, immediately after that.

Starting from the *nābhi* and proceeding clockwise until the point where that *liṅga* fell, one should discard any other [remnants] that have fallen there; having prepared the food, one should worship it. (4) Having completed the departure as before, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa*.

On the right side, with the *puṣpamudrā*, one should offer [the flower] at the heart [of the deity], saying: "Obeisance to Vṛṣabha" (I.56b).

Having worshipped him with the mantra: "We know him who has sharp horns; we meditate upon him whose feet are the Vedas; may that Bull impel us," and having offered incense, lamps, and water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) to all, one should [worship] near the door—those dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, and on earth—with the root mantra for the sake of cutting through the three kinds of obstacles.

Having gazed at the sky with the *divya-dṛṣṭi* [divine vision], one should cast a flower into the atmosphere with the *nārāca-mudrā* while reciting "Astrāya hūṃ phaṭ. Then, having cleansed the ground three times with the left sole of the foot using the *pāśupata-astra*, and having visualized the destruction of the three kinds of obstacles, one should strike the bell with the *astra-mantra*. Having entered inside the half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇṭapa*) by first placing the right foot on the left side of the door while reciting the *sadyojāta* mantra:
Having removed the curtain with the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*), [one should say]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sthāṇu.

Having entered the womb-chamber (*garbhagraha*), one should worship the enclosure of the womb (*garbhāvaraṇa*). (6) At the threshold of the womb-chamber, having worshipped with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), [one should offer] obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site (*vāstvadhipati*), in the direction of Nirṛti;
obeisance to Mahāgaṇapati in the western direction; (7) obeisance to Sarasvatī in the north-western direction; obeisance to Mahālakṣmī in the northern direction.
At the mouth of the cow (gomukha): *oṃ hāṃ vāmāyai namaḥ*. ... At the northeast for the seven gurus (saptaguru): *sadāśivādi-saptagurubhyo namaḥ*.

Then, having worshipped Rudra at the front of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should remove the stale [offerings]. Taking the deity’s remains (*nirmālya*) with the two index fingers (*tarjanī*), and placing a single fresh flower upon the head of the liṅga with the middle and ring fingers, [one recites]: *oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya caṇḍeśvarāya namaḥ*.

Having thus offered the remains of the flowers (*nirmālya*), one should wash the *liṅga* with the water of the *arghya* using the *astra-mantra*, and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with the *pāśupata-mantra*. After the purification of the *liṅga* in this manner, one should perform the purification of the mantra. Visualizing a lotus in the space of one's own seat, and having made a tilaka on the forehead with yellow sandalwood paste, one should recite the *śiva-mantra* ten times while sounding it from the end of *nāda* up to the *suṣumnā* and down to the *mūlādhāra*. One should likewise recite each of the Brahma-aṅgas individually; thus is the purification of the mantra accomplished.
Now, regarding the worship of the seatless [deity]:

one should contemplate Ādhāraśakti at the base— (6) having the color of a jasmine flower or the moon, granting boons, three-eyed, bearing a mass of matted locks, with her right and left hands holding a boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a noose, and a goad— at the root.
Salutation to Ādhāraśakti; above the foundation stone—from the east onwards—salutation to Ananta.

... (I. 57b) But when the fourteenth day is complete and joined with the new moon (*kuhu*), the sin of killing a cow may arise there. In the *Kāmika*: "If the fourteenth day exists at the time of the sun's setting, that night shall be Śivarātri; it would be the most excellent of the excellent."
Lalita said:
"The thirteenth lunar day is full, and the fourteenth is joined with Yama; one should observe a fast on that day with great effort—thus spoke Śambhu. (5)
That night on which the thirteenth lunar day lasts for three watches and the fourteenth lasts for one watch is Śivarātri; one should worship Śiva during that night.
